# Changelog

All notable changes to Token-Goat are documented in this file. Format follows Keep a Changelog. Token-Goat follows Semantic Versioning starting at 1.0.

## [Unreleased]

### Added

- **Kimi Code support.** `token-goat install --kimi` wires token-goat into Moonshot AI's Kimi Code CLI: `[[hooks]]` entries in `~/.kimi-code/config.toml` for `PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`, `PreCompact`, `UserPromptSubmit`, `SubagentStop`, and `SessionStart`, a routing block in `~/.kimi-code/AGENTS.md`, and a skill at `~/.kimi-code/skills/token-goat/SKILL.md`. Kimi Code sends the same snake_case payload Claude Code does, but it reads a different answer: only a top-level `message` and `hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision`. Sending token-goat's own reply would have been read as "allow" every time, so the install writes a shim that translates it, and writes nothing at all for a no-op, because Kimi Code puts raw hook stdout into the model's context on `UserPromptSubmit`. Its read tool names its argument `path`, not `file_path`, so the payload is renamed on the way in as well. `Notification` and `Stop` are not wired: token-goat has no handler for them. Input and output rewriting are not wired either, because Kimi Code offers no channel for them. See [src/bridges/kimi_install.ts](src/bridges/kimi_install.ts) and [src/bridges/kimi.ts](src/bridges/kimi.ts), held by [tests/install_kimi.test.ts](tests/install_kimi.test.ts) and [tests/wire_format_kimi.test.ts](tests/wire_format_kimi.test.ts).
### Security
- **A tracked `.env` handed its secrets to the model.** The non-git directory walk refused to index `.env` and `.env.*`, and said why: they hold secrets, and a bare walk has none of git's exclusions. The reasoning assumed git would have ignored them. git ignores only what `.gitignore` says to ignore, and a tracked `.env` is routine, by intent for `.env.example` and by accident for the real one. On the git path, which is what nearly every project uses, nothing excluded it: the file was chunked and embedded whole, so `token-goat semantic "database connection string"` returned the password as its first result, and `read`, `section`, `symbol`, `pack` and `bash-output --file` all printed it. Values are now replaced with `[REDACTED:dotenv_value]` everywhere Token-Goat stores or prints file text, and key names, which are the useful part and are not secret, are kept. This matches what the symbol index already did: it has always stored env keys with empty bodies. Pattern matching was not enough here, because in this one file type every value is sensitive whatever the key is called, `DEBUG=true` included. See [src/dotenv_redact.ts](src/dotenv_redact.ts), held by [tests/guards/dotenv_values_never_served.test.ts](tests/guards/dotenv_values_never_served.test.ts).
- **An index built before that fix kept serving the old values.** A file is only re-embedded when its bytes change, so redacting from now on would have left every existing install exactly as exposed as before, indefinitely. Opening an index now deletes any chunk belonging to a `.env` file and clears its embedding marker, so the stored text goes and the file is re-read through the redacting path. See [src/db.ts](src/db.ts).
- **Anything unrecognised in a `.env` is now redacted rather than printed.** A shell append, `API_KEY+=more`, was left in the clear on the line below a redacted one, and an unquoted `KEY=head\` continuation put its second half through untouched. Rather than chase each shape, a line in a dotenv file is printed only when it is blank, a comment, or an assignment; everything else is replaced. Cached evidence had the matching hole from the other direction: it ran keyword-based redaction only, so it caught `API_KEY` and kept `DEBUG=true`.
- **A secret in quotes was never redacted.** Redaction runs over every command result, MCP result and cached blob before any of it reaches the model, and it caught `API_KEY=value` but not `API_KEY="value"`. Quotes are how secrets are normally written: `.env` files, JSON, YAML and TOML all quote by default, and a header only ever arrives quoted when a request or response body is logged. So the common shape went through in full and the rare one was covered. Ten realistic shapes were checked and five of them leaked whole, including every JSON body and both `Authorization` headers. The cause was on both sides of the separator: the pattern stopped dead at an opening quote, and the closing quote of a quoted key name blocked it from the other end. Quotes are now allowed around the separator and still refused inside the value, which is what stops a match running past the closing quote. See [src/secret_redact.ts](src/secret_redact.ts), held by [tests/secret_redact.test.ts](tests/secret_redact.test.ts).
- **An OAuth token and a database password went through untouched.** `access_token`, `refresh_token` and `id_token` were not among the names the generic pattern watched, so the credential in a logged token-endpoint response was cached word for word. A connection string had no separator to anchor on at all: `postgres://user:hunter2@db.internal` keeps its password in the authority section, so a `DATABASE_URL` echoed by a failing migration was stored as it stood. Both are covered now. A URL without credentials is left alone, so `http://example.com:8080/path` still reads as it did.
- **A backslash in a value cut the redaction short and left the rest in plain text.** In `{"API_KEY":"abcd\"efghijkl"}` the match stopped at the escaped quote, so `abcd\` was replaced and `efghijkl` stayed readable. A partial redaction is worse than none, because it looks handled. The escape and the character after it are now taken together, and never across a line break, so a value ending in a backslash cannot pull the following line into the match.
- **The redaction pass took four times as long for twice the input.** Nothing here could backtrack, which is the usual test and the one the module documented passing, but a pattern that looks backwards is re-checked at every position it might start from, and two unlimited runs of spaces sat inside one. Text made of the word `password`, eighty thousand spaces and `=!` took 1.7 seconds; twice that took 6.9. This runs on every command result before the model sees it, so a long enough run of spaces could stall it. Those runs are now capped and the same text takes 2 milliseconds. A guard reads the patterns themselves and fails if an unlimited run is ever put back inside one, which does not depend on a stopwatch: see [tests/guards/redaction_lookbehind_bounded.test.ts](tests/guards/redaction_lookbehind_bounded.test.ts).

### Fixed
- **Redacting a secret also deleted what came after it.** The value was allowed to run through a comma or a brace, so `API_KEY=<value>,OTHER=public` lost `,OTHER=public` as well, and the closing brace of an unquoted JSON object went with it. The pattern already refused to cross a space, an `&`, a `;` or a `#` for exactly this reason. It now refuses those three too, so the secret goes and the structure around it stays.

- **`token-goat doctor` said every check passed while warnings were printed above it.** The verdict counted only outright failures, so a run reporting an oversized database, an empty index for the current project and orphaned processes still signed off with `All checks passed` directly under that list. It now says `No failures, but 2 warnings above` instead. What counts as a failure, and the exit code, are unchanged. See [src/cli_doctor.ts](src/cli_doctor.ts), held by [tests/doctor_verdict_warnings.test.ts](tests/doctor_verdict_warnings.test.ts).
- **`token-goat index` counted files it had not indexed.** A file that git still tracks but that no longer exists in the worktree, the state left by a plain `rm` and by every rename until the result is staged, was still listed for indexing. Its fingerprint came back empty, the parser quietly did nothing, and the run counted it anyway. Nothing ever corrected it, because deleting the file is exactly what keeps it in that state, so every later run repeated the same phantom credit. After a rename the effect was plain: `Indexed 1 file into the symbol index` printed by the run that had just emptied the index. The count now reports only files that were really read, and a file already known to be gone is no longer opened at all. See [src/cli.ts](src/cli.ts), held by [tests/cmdindex_vanished_tracked_file.test.ts](tests/cmdindex_vanished_tracked_file.test.ts).
- **The same credit was still possible through a narrower window.** A file present when the check ran could be deleted while its own parse was running, which writes nothing and reports no error. That run is no longer counted either.
- **The six Word and PowerPoint readers passed Node and fflate errors straight through to the user.** Pointing `docx-outline` at a file that was not a zip printed `invalid zip data`, a missing file printed `ENOENT: no such file or directory, stat` followed by the full absolute path the command had resolved on its own, and a directory printed `EISDIR`. Each now says what happened in the caller's own terms: `File not found: report.docx`, or `not a valid .docx file: report.docx`, keeping the original error attached underneath for debugging. The `.xlsx` reader already answered this way, so the two families now agree. See [src/ooxml_extract.ts](src/ooxml_extract.ts), held by [tests/ooxml_extract.test.ts](tests/ooxml_extract.test.ts).
- **The format named in those messages was read off the filename, not off the command.** `docx-outline report.txt` answered `not a valid .txt file`, naming a format nobody had asked about and that the reader could not have read either way. The command knows which format it wants, so it now says so: the same call answers `not a valid .docx file`.
- **Any failure to open the file was reported as a missing file.** A permission error told the reader to go looking for a file that was sitting exactly where they left it. Only a genuinely absent file is now called missing; anything else names the error it actually hit.
## [2.6.32] - 2026-08-18

### Security
- **Dependabot proposed a new version the day it was published, and watched only the action pins.** The npm tree was not watched at all, so every dependency advisory here waited on somebody noticing it, and the extension's own lockfile was watched by nobody. Both manifests are now covered, and every entry has a seven-day `cooldown`. That window is the control that matters for npm: the account-takeover pattern is a bad version published, installed by whoever updates first, and yanked hours later. Waiting does not make a package safe, it means somebody else finds out first. See [.github/dependabot.yml](.github/dependabot.yml), held by [tests/guards/dependabot_coverage.test.ts](tests/guards/dependabot_coverage.test.ts).
- **Workflows ran on whatever token the repository handed them.** Neither CI nor the publish workflow declared a top-level `permissions:` block, so every job in them inherited the repository default, which on many repositories is a writable `GITHUB_TOKEN`. Nobody had chosen that. Both now default to `contents: read`, and the publish job keeps declaring the one extra permission it needs, `id-token: write` for npm provenance, in the open where it can be read. An infrastructure scan flagged this as CKV2_GHA_1 and it now reports nothing. See [.github/workflows/ci.yml](.github/workflows/ci.yml) and [.github/workflows/publish.yml](.github/workflows/publish.yml), held by [tests/guards/workflow_permissions.test.ts](tests/guards/workflow_permissions.test.ts).

### Changed
- **Three packages with no license grant at all left the dependency tree.** `buffers@0.1.1` and `chainsaw@0.1.0` shipped with neither a `license` field nor a license file, and `traverse@0.3.9` had the file but not the field. For a license review no grant is worse than a copyleft grant, because there is nothing to apply a policy to. All three arrived through `exceljs`, which depends on `unzipper`, which depended on `binary`, which depended on all three; `unzipper` dropped `binary` in 0.11, so an override to `^0.12.5` removes the sub-chain and the deprecated `fstream` with it. What cannot be removed is now written down instead: [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) names every remaining production package a scanner cannot resolve or that carries a copyleft term, what it actually grants, and the fact that all of them are optional. Held by [tests/guards/dependency_licenses.test.ts](tests/guards/dependency_licenses.test.ts).
- **Five transitive packages are pinned to patched versions, and the limit of that is written down.** [package.json](package.json) now carries an `overrides` block for `protobufjs`, `deepmerge-ts`, `uuid`, `sharp` and `unzipper`, which takes `npm audit` on this repository to nothing. npm applies overrides only in the project you run it from, so they do not travel to anyone who installs Token-Goat as a dependency, and a clean scan of this repository is therefore not a clean scan of an install. Rather than let the better number stand on its own, [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) now gives all three answers -- repository, install without optional packages, default install -- with the command that reproduces each.
- **A secrets scan of this repository reported 26 findings, all of them test fixtures.** Token-Goat redacts secrets out of command output, so its tests are full of things shaped like secrets: AWS's own documented example key, GitHub tokens written as split strings of keyboard runs, private-key blocks whose body is the literal text `first-key-body`. A new [.gitleaks.toml](.gitleaks.toml) records why those paths are allowed and scopes the allowance to tests and to directories that are not this project's source. It deliberately does not cover `src/`, so a credential committed where the shipping code lives still fails the scan.
- **`npm run sbom` writes a CycloneDX bill of materials.** For a scanner that reads a bill of materials rather than a lockfile.
- **The build tooling carried two advisories of its own.** A scan reads a lockfile whole, so a finding against a development dependency lands the same as one against a shipped package. esbuild moved from 0.24 to 0.28, which clears an advisory about its development server (a server Token-Goat never starts: esbuild is used as a library to produce the bundle), and the eslint chain brought in a version of brace-expansion with three denial-of-service advisories. `npm audit` including development dependencies now reports nothing. The bundle is unchanged in shape: the split-output and built-artifact tests run against the real file.

- **The one advisory left in an install without optional packages is gone, and that install is now clean.** `html-to-text` was listed as a runtime dependency and brought `deepmerge-ts` with it, along with `htmlparser2`, `selderee` and `dom-serializer`. It never needed to be: the build inlines it into the shipped bundle, and nothing in the published files imports the package, so every consumer downloaded five packages that no code would ever load. It is a development dependency now. `npm install --omit=optional token-goat` followed by `npm audit` reports nothing across 46 packages, where it used to report one chain. The text a fetched page is reduced to is byte-for-byte what it was, checked against the packed tarball rather than against the repository. See [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md), held by [tests/guards/dependency_advisory_disclosure.test.ts](tests/guards/dependency_advisory_disclosure.test.ts).

### Fixed
- **Installing without optional packages produced a program that could not run at all.** [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) recommends `npm install --omit=optional` to avoid the advisories in the native packages, and that install could not answer `token-goat --version`: it stopped on a missing `fflate`. Every other reader of an optional package loads it only when something asks for it, but the zip reader imported it at the top of the file, which puts it on the path Node resolves before any command starts. One optional package missing therefore took out all of them. It is loaded on demand now, and `zip-list` and `zip-read` say the package is missing instead of claiming the archive is corrupt, which is what they used to say and sent the reader to look at a file that was fine. A guard reads the built bundle rather than the source, because a top-level import is what the failure actually was: see [tests/guards/optional_deps_are_lazy.test.ts](tests/guards/optional_deps_are_lazy.test.ts) and [src/archive_query.ts](src/archive_query.ts).
- **An allow list written with a non-English domain name refused every URL.** A URL parser stores an internationalised host in its punycode form, because that is what DNS is asked for, and nothing turned it back. So `webfetch.allow` written as an operator would actually type it matched no host at all and quietly blocked every request to that host. The two spellings are now interchangeable, the same way a default port already was. The widening decodes that exact hostname and nothing else, so a look-alike domain built from a different character is still a different host and is still refused. See [src/url_policy.ts](src/url_policy.ts) and [tests/url_policy_canonicalization.test.ts](tests/url_policy_canonicalization.test.ts).
- **The package declared its license in the form that scanners cannot resolve.** Both manifests and both lockfiles said `SEE LICENSE IN LICENSE`. That is npm's documented form for a license with no SPDX identifier, and this license has one: `PolyForm-Noncommercial-1.0.0` is on the SPDX list. The difference matters to the reader the field exists for. A declared identifier resolves to a known license and a scanner applies policy to it on its own; the pointer form resolves to nothing and arrives as an unknown license needing manual review, which is slower and more likely to end in a refusal by default. All four files now declare the identifier. The grant is unchanged and the terms are unchanged: commercial use still requires a license, and the point is to be identified correctly as noncommercial rather than to look permissive. See [tests/guards/license_declaration_matches.test.ts](tests/guards/license_declaration_matches.test.ts).
- **Excluding a directory left everything already indexed under it readable.** `token-goat project exclude <path>` stopped future indexing and did nothing about what was already there, so a directory of credentials excluded after a first index kept its symbol bodies in the database and kept answering `symbol` queries. Pruning could not have caught it either: pruning removes rows for files that are gone from disk, and an excluded file is still on disk, which is the whole point. Excluding a path now removes what was indexed under it and says how many files went, and a full `index` run purges a blocked file rather than quietly skipping past the rows it left behind. Confirmed by indexing a directory, excluding it, and watching the body come straight back. See [src/index_prune.ts](src/index_prune.ts), tested in [tests/blocked_root_purge.test.ts](tests/blocked_root_purge.test.ts).
- **Prune matched paths by case but not by separator.** Every root arrives forward-slashed while a row written from a raw operating-system path keeps its backslashes, and the comparison lowercased both without normalizing either, so such a row was invisible to every prefix-scoped scan and reported as nothing to do. See [src/index_prune.ts](src/index_prune.ts).


## [2.6.31] - 2026-08-18

### Security
- **A repository could switch off token-goat's security controls just by shipping a config file.** A project-root `.token-goat.toml` layers on top of the global config, which is what it is for: hint thresholds, indexing settings, compression tuning. But that file arrives with the repository, so it is written by whoever wrote the repository. A checked-in three-line file could turn off prompt-injection fencing, empty the fetch allow and deny lists, switch the Google Drive integration back on, widen the MCP root allowlist, or lift the confinement that keeps `symbol` inside one project, silently, for every session anyone opened in that directory. Confirmed by cloning a directory with such a file and watching a hostile result come through unwrapped. Those five settings now come from the global config and the environment only, and a project file that tries to set one is ignored with a message naming what was dropped. The environment is deliberately left alone: a repository cannot set it, and a developer exporting a variable is configuring their own machine. Everything else stays project-overridable. See [src/config.ts](src/config.ts), regression-tested in [tests/project_config_locked_sections.test.ts](tests/project_config_locked_sections.test.ts).
- **A hostile MCP server could get its prompt injection through unwrapped by making the call fail, or by making it twice.** MCP results are scanned for prompt-injection phrasing and wrapped in a marker saying the text inside is data, not instructions. The scan sat below three shortcuts that exist to save work: one for a result the server flagged as an error, one for a call that carried no session id, and one for a call whose result was already cached. Each returned before the scan ran, so a server only had to satisfy one of the three -- flag its own reply as an error, or simply be called a second time -- and the payload arrived unmarked. The scan now runs before any of the three, so a caching shortcut can no longer double as a way around the wrapper. See [src/hooks_mcp.ts](src/hooks_mcp.ts), regression-tested in [tests/hooks_mcp.test.ts](tests/hooks_mcp.test.ts).
- **A symlink walked straight out of the directory `symbol` was confined to.** Confining `symbol` to one project compares the requested path against the project root as text. A link inside the project pointing at a directory outside it produced a path that reads as inside while naming a file that is not, so the confinement passed and the file outside was returned. The check now resolves links before comparing. The same check also assumed a Windows-only rule for when upper and lower case mean the same path, which wrongly rejected legitimate paths on macOS; it now asks the filesystem. See [src/project.ts](src/project.ts), regression-tested in [tests/codex_review_regressions.test.ts](tests/codex_review_regressions.test.ts).
- **The untrusted-content wrapper could be closed with a slightly malformed tag.** Content is wrapped in a marker so the model can tell where untrusted text starts and ends, and any copy of that marker inside the content is escaped so the content cannot close the wrapper early. `</untrusted-tool-output/>` is malformed but still reads as a closing tag, and it was not escaped. It is now. See [src/injection_scan.ts](src/injection_scan.ts).
- **A presigned download link was not recognised as a secret.** A presigned url is a password in url form: anyone holding the whole link can read or write the object until it expires. None of the existing patterns matched one, because the signature has no distinctive prefix, so presigned links passed through cached output and fetched pages in plain text. AWS, Google Cloud Storage and Azure signature parameters are now redacted. See [src/secret_redact.ts](src/secret_redact.ts).
- **A prompt sent with a fetched page was stored in the session file unredacted, and two links differing only in their key were treated as one.** Only the url half of the stored entry was redacted, so a token pasted into the prompt stayed on disk in full. Redacting alone also merged two links that differ only inside the redacted part, which returned the wrong cached page and dropped a fetch from the compaction summary. Both halves are now redacted and an identity marker keeps the entries distinct. Entries written by an older version are rewritten into the new shape when the file is read, so an old file stops carrying credentials instead of keeping them for the life of the session. See [src/session.ts](src/session.ts) and [src/session_store.ts](src/session_store.ts).
- **Download and fetch urls were written to the session file with their credentials intact.** Every cache token-goat writes goes through a redaction pass on the way to disk, but the per-session state file is written directly and skips it. Two of its fields hold urls: the list of `curl -o` downloads and the list of fetched pages. A url carries credentials as readily as output does, so `curl -o data.json "https://api.example.com/export?api_key=sk-live-..."` put a live key in plain text in that file, as did a signed link with its signature. Confirmed by running the hook and reading the file. The two are fixed differently because they are used differently: the fetched-url list is redacted, since the compaction manifest displays it and it needs to stay readable, and the download list is keyed by a digest of the url, since its only consumer is an exact-match check that blocks a repeat download and a redaction there would make two urls differing only in their key look like the same download. See [src/session.ts](src/session.ts), regression-tested in [tests/session_state_url_secrets.test.ts](tests/session_state_url_secrets.test.ts).
- **MCP tool results were never checked for prompt injection, on any path.** The injection scan covered fetched web pages only. An MCP result is a remote server's output, which makes it the least trustworthy text token-goat handles, and it was scanned nowhere: not when it arrived, and not when a cached copy was recalled. A compromised or hostile MCP server could put "ignore all previous instructions" straight into the model's context with nothing marking it as untrusted, on the very hook token-goat already uses to rewrite that output. MCP results are now scanned as they arrive and fenced on a match, independently of the compression path, so a short hostile result is covered even though it is too small to be worth compressing and even with compression switched off. Recall of cached Bash and MCP output is scanned too: the output of a build or test run in a project with a hostile dependency is third-party text just as a web page is, and the recall channel served it unmarked. The fence for tool output carries its own tag, so the label names where the text came from. A fence only appears when a pattern matches, so ordinary output is byte-identical to before. See [src/hooks_mcp.ts](src/hooks_mcp.ts), [src/cli.ts](src/cli.ts) and [src/injection_scan.ts](src/injection_scan.ts), regression-tested in [tests/hooks_mcp.test.ts](tests/hooks_mcp.test.ts) and [tests/cli_web_output_injection_fence.test.ts](tests/cli_web_output_injection_fence.test.ts).
- **`symbol` read out of every project on the machine, and a directory sandbox did not stop it.** The symbol index is one machine-wide database keyed by absolute path, and `symbol` queries it rather than the current project. From any indexed folder, `token-goat symbol <name>` returned the matching function and its full body from any other repository indexed on that host, and `symbol --grep .` listed all of them. Confining an agent to one directory did not close this, because the answer came from the index and never touched the files it was kept away from. This is useful on a personal machine and is still the default, but there was no way to turn it off. Setting `indexing.cross_project_symbols = false` (env `TOKEN_GOAT_CROSS_PROJECT_SYMBOLS`) now confines `symbol` to the project it runs in, and a `--project` or `--file` argument pointing outside that project is refused instead of honored, so the setting cannot be undone from inside the process it constrains. See [src/read_commands.ts](src/read_commands.ts) and [src/project.ts](src/project.ts), regression-tested in [tests/symbol_cross_project_confinement.test.ts](tests/symbol_cross_project_confinement.test.ts).
- **A deny pattern could be stepped around by rewriting the same address.** Allow and deny patterns were compared against the address exactly as typed, so several different spellings of one request went straight through a rule written to stop it: a trailing dot on the site name (`https://example.com./private/x`, which reaches the same server), `..` or `.` segments in the path that the browser removes before sending, the port number written out when it is the default one, and `%70rivate` in place of `private`. Each reaches exactly the page the rule named. Worse, the more carefully a rule was written the easier it was to sidestep: a loose `*example.com*` still caught all of them, so only precise rules failed. Patterns are now compared against the address as it will actually be sent, as well as the text as typed. Separately, writing out a default port in a rule (`https://example.com:443/*`) matched no site at all, so an allow list written that way refused everything and a deny list written that way quietly stopped covering the site; the two spellings are now interchangeable. See [src/url_policy.ts](src/url_policy.ts), regression-tested in [tests/url_policy_canonicalization.test.ts](tests/url_policy_canonicalization.test.ts).
- **The headless browser ignored the `webfetch.allow`/`webfetch.deny` policy.** `token-goat screenshot` launches Chromium and navigates on its own, so it was the one outbound channel the egress policy never reached: an install configured to deny everything still rendered any address it was handed and wrote the image to disk. The check now runs in the same function that already vets every redirect hop and every sub-resource the page loads, so a denied host is unreachable as an image, script, or iframe source too, not just as the page being captured. The refusal names the policy without echoing the URL's query string, so a signed screenshot link cannot leak its token into the error text. See [src/screenshot.ts](src/screenshot.ts), regression-tested in [tests/screenshot_egress_policy.test.ts](tests/screenshot_egress_policy.test.ts).
- **The cache and index directory was readable by every user on the machine.** Everything token-goat stores lands under one directory: command output, fetched pages, MCP results, session state, and the searchable index of your source. It was created with a plain recursive mkdir, so it took the system default, which on a stock Linux box means any other local user could list and read it. Measured on Linux before the fix: mode 755. It is now created owner-only, and an existing directory is tightened on the next run, so a colleague sharing the same build box cannot read your cached work. Shared parent folders such as `~/.local/share` are deliberately left alone, since they belong to every application and not to token-goat. No effect on Windows, which uses inherited ACLs rather than these permissions. See [src/constants.ts](src/constants.ts), regression-tested in [tests/data_dir_permissions.test.ts](tests/data_dir_permissions.test.ts).
- **The Google Drive integration can now be switched off completely.** `gdrive-sections` is the only command that talks to Google, and there was no way to remove it: it was always runnable, and the routing guidance token-goat writes into CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, `copilot-instructions.md` and the installed skill always named it, so every agent was told the command existed even at an organisation that does not use Drive. Setting `gdrive.enabled = false` (env `TOKEN_GOAT_GDRIVE_ENABLED`) now refuses the command before it opens a connection and drops it from all four guidance surfaces, so the feature is neither reachable nor visible. It stays on by default, so existing installs are unchanged. See [src/config.ts](src/config.ts) and [src/bridges/guidance_block.ts](src/bridges/guidance_block.ts), regression-tested in [tests/gdrive_disable_gate.test.ts](tests/gdrive_disable_gate.test.ts).
- **The `webfetch.allow`/`webfetch.deny` policy did not apply to token-goat's own two outbound commands.** The setting decides which sites may be fetched, and it was checked in one place only: the hook that gates your AI's WebFetch tool. `fetch-image` and `gdrive-sections` open their own connections and skipped the check entirely, so an install configured to deny everything still had two commands that reached the internet. Confirmed on a real install with `deny = ["*"]`: `gdrive-sections` still reached Google and `fetch-image` still downloaded a file. The check now lives at the single point every fetch token-goat makes itself goes through, so both commands obey it, as will anything added later, and each redirect hop is checked too, which stops an allowed site redirecting the request on to a denied one. Deny beats allow, and a non-empty allow list refuses anything it does not name. Both lists can now also be set with `TOKEN_GOAT_WEBFETCH_ALLOW` and `TOKEN_GOAT_WEBFETCH_DENY` (comma-separated), so a container or CI job can pin the policy without shipping a config file: an organisation that does not use Google Drive can deny `*docs.google.com*` and be certain nothing here contacts it. Both lists stay empty by default, so an install that has not configured them is unchanged. See [src/webfetch.ts](src/webfetch.ts), [src/url_policy.ts](src/url_policy.ts) and [src/config.ts](src/config.ts), regression-tested in [tests/webfetch_policy_enforcement.test.ts](tests/webfetch_policy_enforcement.test.ts).
- **A page that was wrapped as untrusted when fetched came back unwrapped when read again from the cache.** Every fetched page is scanned for prompt-injection patterns and, on a match, wrapped in a marker telling the model the text inside is data and not instructions. Reading the same page back with `token-goat web-output <id>` skipped that entirely and printed the stored body bare, which is the recall token-goat itself points the model at, so the attack text reached the model without its wrapper. The recall now runs the same scan and wraps what it prints. It scans the slice the caller actually gets, so a `--grep` or `--head` that keeps the attack text is wrapped and one that filters it out is not, and the `injection.enabled` setting still turns the whole thing off. Cached command output and cached tool results are left alone, since neither is a fetched page. See [src/cli.ts](src/cli.ts), regression-tested in [tests/cli_web_output_injection_fence.test.ts](tests/cli_web_output_injection_fence.test.ts).
- **Secrets were left in plain text whenever the key name only contained the word, such as `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=`.** Cached command output, MCP results and fetched pages are scanned for secrets before anything is stored or handed back, and the catch-all rule for `name=value` lines required the word `password`, `secret` or `api_key` to sit immediately before the `=` or `:`. The standard spelling of an AWS secret access key does not, nor does `SECRET_KEY=`, `DB_PASSWORD_HASH=` or any other name where the word is a prefix rather than the whole of it, so all of them were kept and searchable in full. The spellings `apikey=` and `api-key=` were missed as well. The rule now allows the word to be part of a longer name, and covers those two spellings. Text that merely mentions one of the words is still left alone, because the name must still run into a `=` or `:` to count. See [src/secret_redact.ts](src/secret_redact.ts), regression-tested in [tests/secret_redact.test.ts](tests/secret_redact.test.ts).
- **Several kinds of internal address were not recognised as internal when fetching a URL.** Token-goat refuses to fetch an address that points somewhere private, so a page or a prompt cannot talk it into reaching a machine on your own network. Eight kinds of address got past that check: multicast (`224.0.0.1`), the broadcast address and the rest of the reserved top of the range, the benchmarking range, the block reserved for protocol assignments, the deprecated site-local IPv6 range, IPv6 multicast, and two standard ways of carrying an IPv4 address inside an IPv6 one, 6to4 and NAT64, which meant `2002:7f00:1::` and `64:ff9b::7f00:1` both reached `127.0.0.1` on a machine set up for either. The two IPv6 wrappers are checked by the address they carry, exactly as the already-handled `::ffff:` form is, so a public address inside one is still reachable. See [src/webfetch.ts](src/webfetch.ts), regression-tested in [tests/webfetch.test.ts](tests/webfetch.test.ts).
- **Fetched content could close its own "this is untrusted" fence by changing the capitalisation.** Web and file content that token-goat hands to the model is wrapped in a marker saying the text inside is data and not instructions, and any copy of that marker inside the content itself is escaped so the content cannot close the wrapper early and make the rest of itself look like it came from outside. Only the exact lower-case spelling was escaped. `</UNTRUSTED-WEB-CONTENT>`, `</Untrusted-Web-Content>`, the same tag with a space before the bracket, and the same tag carrying an attribute all went through untouched, and each reads as that same closing marker: the one spelling that was covered is the only one an attacker had no reason to write. The escaping now ignores capitalisation and allows the spacing and attributes a tag can carry. Ordinary angle brackets in the content are still left alone. See [src/injection_scan.ts](src/injection_scan.ts), regression-tested in [tests/injection_scan.test.ts](tests/injection_scan.test.ts).
- **A web address could get past the allow list by mentioning an allowed site anywhere in it.** The allow and deny lists were compared against the whole address as one piece of text, so an allowed name only had to appear somewhere inside it. With an allow list of `https://*.example.com/*`, the address `https://evil.com/steal?x=.example.com/` passed, and the request still went to `evil.com`: the allowed name sat in the query, which is the part an attacker writes. That defeats the point of the setting, which is to stop an agent sending anything anywhere but the sites you named. A deny list had the mirror problem: `https://someone@evil.com/` reached `evil.com` while dodging a `https://evil.com/*` deny rule, because the text no longer matched. Both lists now also check the site the address really contacts, taken from the address itself rather than from where a name happens to appear in the text. Allowing is stricter, denying is broader, and a deny rule written for one path stays on that path. See [src/hooks_fetch.ts](src/hooks_fetch.ts), regression-tested in [tests/hooks_fetch.test.ts](tests/hooks_fetch.test.ts).
- **A redirect from a secure page to an insecure one on the same site kept the caller's credentials.** Headers a caller supplies, such as an API key, are only meant to follow a redirect that stays on the same site, and the test for that compared the host name and port but not whether the address was still `https`. A server could answer with a redirect to the plain `http` version of itself and be handed the same key, sending it across the network unencrypted at a destination the server chooses. The test now compares the full origin, which includes `https` as well as the host and port. No caller ships credentials through this path today, so nothing was exposed, but the guard was not doing what it said. See [src/webfetch.ts](src/webfetch.ts), regression-tested in [tests/webfetch.test.ts](tests/webfetch.test.ts).

### Added
- **Nothing said how to check that the package on npm came from this repository.** It always did: publishing runs from one workflow, only when a GitHub release is published, with npm provenance, and every action it uses is pinned to a commit rather than a tag. None of that was written down, so the answer to a supply-chain review was "read the workflow yourself". [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) now has a Verifying what you installed section naming `npm audit signatures`, and a test keeps the claim and the workflow from drifting apart.
- **`.tokengoatignore` looked like it kept files out of the index. It never did.** The file is read in exactly one place, `token-goat pack`, but the README said `index` honoured it and that `ignores` listed its patterns, so someone keeping a directory of credentials out of the index reached for the file named "ignore", saw no error, and got the directory indexed anyway: confirmed by excluding a directory and watching `symbol` return its contents. `ignores` now reports the file and says what it applies to, and names `token-goat project exclude <path>`, which is the setting that genuinely stops indexing. The README says the same. See [src/text_commands.ts](src/text_commands.ts), tested in [tests/ignores_pack_scope.test.ts](tests/ignores_pack_scope.test.ts).
- **`token-goat doctor` now reports the security posture in one place.** Answering "what is this allowed to reach on my machine, and who else can read what it stored" meant reading the config file, the README, and a directory mode nobody looks at. `doctor` now prints a Security section: offline mode, injection scanning, the Google Drive integration, whether fetching runs against an allow list or only a deny list, whether MCP reads stay inside the project root, and the data directory's permissions. It only warns when a protection that ships on has been turned off, so a default install stays quiet. See [src/cli_doctor.ts](src/cli_doctor.ts), tested in [tests/doctor_security_posture.test.ts](tests/doctor_security_posture.test.ts).
- **`token-goat uninstall --purge` deletes the data directories too.** Uninstall deliberately left them alone, which is right for a reinstall and wrong for offboarding a machine: the README said to remove them by hand, and there are two roots that sit somewhere different on every platform. `--purge` removes both, naming each one and how much it reclaimed, and refuses while the worker is running rather than deleting files it is about to rewrite. The default is unchanged. See [src/purge.ts](src/purge.ts), tested in [tests/purge.test.ts](tests/purge.test.ts).
- **`network.offline`: one switch that stops token-goat opening any connection of its own.** Answering "what does this talk to" previously meant auditing five separate paths, and one of them was undocumented: the automatic text extraction from images downloads its English language data from a CDN the first time it runs, which the security section's list of outbound cases did not mention. That list is now complete, and `network.offline = true` (env `TOKEN_GOAT_OFFLINE`) makes every one of those paths refuse instead of connecting: token-goat's own HTTP fetches, the embedding-model download, the language-data download, and `screenshot`. Each says it is offline rather than failing quietly. Anything already cached still works, so an air-gapped machine with the model and language data in place keeps both semantic search and image text. Offline mode is one of the settings a per-project config file may not set. See [src/config.ts](src/config.ts), regression-tested in [tests/network_offline.test.ts](tests/network_offline.test.ts).

### Fixed
- **The published package did not carry the security document its own README links to.** `files` listed `dist/`, `README.md`, and `LICENSE`, so the tarball had no `SECURITY.md`. npm rewrites relative links on its own page, but anyone reviewing the extracted package, which is what a procurement or supply-chain review actually looks at, followed the dependency-advisory link to nothing. It ships now, and a guard test keeps the link and the packed file together.
- **A plain `token-goat uninstall` left other harnesses wired and said nothing about it.** Integrations for Codex, Copilot, Gemini, Qwen, pi, opencode, OpenClaw, and Grok are removed only when their flag is passed, which is a reasonable default: uninstall should not silently undo something you did not ask about. What was not reasonable was the silence. Installing with `--codex` and then running a plain `uninstall` printed three "Removed" lines and left the Codex config entries, the AGENTS.md block, and the shim script in place, all pointing at a binary that is about to be deleted. Offboarding a machine is exactly when nobody looks twice, and a Copilot `preToolUse` hook whose target is gone fails closed on every call in that session. Uninstall now names each integration still installed and the flag that removes it, the same way it already reports a stray CLAUDE.md block instead of editing a file it does not own. A malformed config belonging to another harness is skipped rather than allowed to abort the uninstall. See [src/cli.ts](src/cli.ts), tested in [tests/uninstall_leftover_integrations.test.ts](tests/uninstall_leftover_integrations.test.ts).
- **The README's list of what changes cited internals from before the TypeScript rewrite.** The crash-safety row named Python exception types; the dirty-queue row credited an `fcntl`/`msvcrt` file lock that does not exist, when what actually prevents a corrupt entry is that each append is one line and an append following a torn write starts with a newline; and one row was not a behaviour at all but a note about a Python-era refactor, naming helpers that no longer exist. All three now describe the shipped code, and the refactor note is gone.
- **The README described the hook's crash safety in a language this project no longer uses.** The row explaining what happens when a hook crashes said a "fail-soft barrier catches `BaseException`/`MemoryError`/`SystemExit`", which are Python exception names left over from before the TypeScript rewrite, and named a return shape the shim does not emit. The behaviour itself is right and was confirmed by running the installed shim against a broken environment and against stdin that is not JSON: both print `{}` and exit 0, so the tool call proceeds untouched. The row now lists the five ways the shim can fail and what each does. This matters more than a wording nit because a `preToolUse` hook that crashes is fail-closed in at least one harness, where it blocks the whole session rather than one call. Tests now spawn the generated shim for each reachable case, including a token-goat child that prints a half-written decision and then exits non-zero, which must not be honoured. See [README.md](README.md), tested in [tests/bridges/shims.test.ts](tests/bridges/shims.test.ts).
- **The README said install grants the agent unprompted shell execution. It does not.** The "what gets installed" table listed a `Bash(token-goat:*)` permission allowlist entry in `settings.json`, and the Claude Code section repeated it. Nothing in the installer has ever written one: a fresh install produces a `settings.json` whose only key is `hooks`, confirmed by running it into an empty home and reading the file. That claim reads exactly like the thing an enterprise review is looking for, an installer quietly granting an agent the right to run any subcommand -- `write-file` and `fetch-image` among them -- without an approval prompt, and it was never true. Both places now say what actually happens, and whether those commands need a prompt is left to your own settings, untouched. Two tests check the written file rather than the intention, including that a permission block you already had comes back byte-identical. See [README.md](README.md), tested in [tests/install.test.ts](tests/install.test.ts).
- **The README said what the index is called, not what it holds.** "Contains the symbol index" reads like a list of names and line numbers. It is not: the database stores the source text of every indexed symbol, its doc comment, the line around each reference, and the passages semantic search embeds, plus a full-text index over the bodies. That is a substantial copy of the source, in a plain unencrypted SQLite file outside the repository, in a directory that on Linux and macOS sits under a home that backup and sync tools routinely copy. Anyone evaluating the tool has to know that before they decide, so the README now says it plainly, names the columns, and says what follows: no telemetry and nothing that carries index content leaves the machine, the repository's access controls no longer apply to it, and it outlives an uninstall unless you pass `--purge`. A guard test freezes the table list, so a new content-bearing table cannot land without a decision about what the document has to say. See [README.md](README.md), tested in [tests/guards/index_contents_disclosure.test.ts](tests/guards/index_contents_disclosure.test.ts).
- **The README advertised a Node version nothing was tested on.** It said the tests run on Node.js 20 and 22, while `package.json` requires 22 or later and every CI job pins 22, so anyone building a support matrix from the README got a version that has never been run. It now describes what actually happens: the full suite on Node.js 22 across Windows, macOS, and Linux, all three gating. A guard test keeps the three statements agreeing. See [README.md](README.md), tested in [tests/guards/node_support_claims_agree.test.ts](tests/guards/node_support_claims_agree.test.ts).
- **Twenty advisories in the runtime dependencies, and no statement about the ones that remain.** `npm audit --omit=dev` reported twenty findings on the published package, one of them critical. Eleven cleared by taking the patches already available, and two more by moving `sharp` and `puppeteer-core` across a major version each rather than leaving them pinned below their fix. The nine that remain all trace to three packages that are already at their latest published version, where npm's only suggested fix is a downgrade to an older major that drops features token-goat uses. Silence about those was the real problem for anyone reviewing the package, so SECURITY.md now names each one, says where it loads, and says why it does or does not reach you: two are optional and an install can simply not have them, and the third is reachable only through an options object token-goat writes itself. A guard test keeps the manifest and that document from drifting apart. See [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md), tested in [tests/guards/dependency_advisory_disclosure.test.ts](tests/guards/dependency_advisory_disclosure.test.ts).
- **The package declared the wrong license.** `package.json` said `MIT` while LICENSE, the README badge, and SECURITY.md all said PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0. Every license scanner, SBOM generator, and legal review reads the `package.json` field, so the published package told them it was permissive when it is not. It now says `SEE LICENSE IN LICENSE`, which is npm's form for a license with no SPDX identifier, and a guard test keeps the two from drifting apart again. SECURITY.md also asked reporters for their Python version, left over from before the TypeScript rewrite.
- **Workflow actions ran from mutable tags.** `actions/checkout@v4` and its siblings resolve through a tag the action's owner can repoint at any commit. The publish workflow was already pinned to commit SHAs; CI and Pages were not, and Pages holds `pages: write` and `id-token: write`. All of them are pinned now, with the version in a comment beside each SHA, a guard test that fails on a new unpinned reference, and a Dependabot schedule so the pins do not go stale. See [.github/workflows](.github/workflows).
- **`token-goat doctor` reported a clean bill of health when it could not read the process list at all.** The Windows process gather returned an empty list both when the machine genuinely had nothing to report and when the PowerShell call timed out, so a failed check printed "no duplicate MCP launchers or orphaned Node processes detected" backed by no data. It now returns nothing at all in the failure case and doctor says the list could not be read. The timeout also went from 5 to 20 seconds, which is what made it fail intermittently on a loaded machine in the first place. See [src/cli_doctor.ts](src/cli_doctor.ts).
- **A permissions test could never pass on Linux or macOS, so CI was red.** The test that checks token-goat does not tighten the shared parent directories above its data root asserted that the enclosing temporary directory was group-readable. A temporary directory made by `mkdtemp` is owner-only by definition, so the assertion was impossible and the job failed on both POSIX runners while Windows skipped the test entirely. It now compares against a reference directory created in the same process, which carries whatever umask the machine has, and separately checks the pre-existing ancestor is left exactly as it was found. See [tests/data_dir_permissions.test.ts](tests/data_dir_permissions.test.ts).
- **The "you rewrote a file you could have edited" hint reported the wrong line count and the wrong percentage.** Splitting text on newlines leaves an empty piece at the end when the text ends in a newline, which nearly every file does, and both numbers in the hint were counted from those pieces. A 40-line file was described as a "41-line file", and because the empty piece at the end of the old content always matched the one at the end of the new content, it added a free unchanged line: thirty of forty lines kept was reported as 76% unchanged instead of 75%. The same inflated count was compared against the setting for the smallest file worth mentioning, so a file one line short of it was treated as long enough. Both numbers are now the file's real ones. See [src/hooks_write.ts](src/hooks_write.ts), regression-tested in [tests/hooks_write.test.ts](tests/hooks_write.test.ts).
- **A failed web search was cached, and every retry of it was blocked.** Repeating a web search within the session points the model at the cached result instead of searching again. Results that come back as errors, such as a rate limit, were cached the same way, so the next identical search was refused and the model was handed the error message to read rather than being allowed to try again, for as long as the cache entry lived. The rule against caching an error was already written down and applied to MCP tool results; web search wrote into the same cache without it. The check now lives next to the function that reads a tool's result, where both callers see it. See [src/hooks_websearch.ts](src/hooks_websearch.ts) and [src/hooks_common.ts](src/hooks_common.ts), regression-tested in [tests/hooks_websearch.test.ts](tests/hooks_websearch.test.ts).
- **The test-only batch mode let one command's environment variables reach the next command.** Serving many invocations from one process is only safe while each is indistinguishable from a separately started one, so the server restores the environment between them. It only did so when the request carried an environment of its own; when it did not, nothing was saved and so nothing was put back, and a variable the command set itself, as `hook --harness` does, stayed set for every later command in that process. The environment is now saved and restored either way. See [src/batch_serve.ts](src/batch_serve.ts), regression-tested in [tests/batch_serve_equivalence.test.ts](tests/batch_serve_equivalence.test.ts).
- **`todo` reported ordinary sentences containing the word "note" as markers.** The scan matched marker names without regard to case, which is right for `// todo: fix this` but also matches "note" and "hack" as the everyday English words they are, so any prose containing "a note for this" or "please note that" was listed as a marker. On this repository that was 681 of 800 reported markers, nearly all of them changelog sentences, which buries the real ones the command exists to surface. A marker is now recognised when it is written in upper case, or when it carries the colon that marks it as a label rather than a word in a sentence, so `// TODO fix this` and `// todo: fix this` are both still found and "a note for this" is not. The same repository now reports 218 markers, none of them prose. See [src/text_commands.ts](src/text_commands.ts), regression-tested in [tests/text_commands.test.ts](tests/text_commands.test.ts).
- **`mcp-audit` reported thousands of tokens of cost for a server that does not exist.** The audit reads the cache of MCP tool results, takes the server name out of each entry's label, and bills the cost against it. Two things go into that cache besides real MCP calls: sub-agent results and web-search results, both stored there so `recall` can find them. Neither has a server name in its label, so both fell into a catch-all row called `unknown` and were reported as MCP server cost. On this machine every one of the 43 cached entries was one of those two, so the entire report, 63597 tokens, was cost attributed to a server that was never called. The report now covers only entries that name a server, and says "none" when there are none. Separately, the server name was matched against a fixed set of characters that excluded the dot, though a server name is a key in `.mcp.json` and may contain one: a server named `my.server` appeared twice, once from the configuration with no calls and once as unattributed cost, instead of once with its real cost. Names are now read up to the separator that ends them, whatever they contain. See [src/cli_mcp_audit.ts](src/cli_mcp_audit.ts), regression-tested in [tests/cli_mcp_audit.test.ts](tests/cli_mcp_audit.test.ts).
- **An approved plan of one or two words could delete an unrelated result body.** After a plan is approved the result echoes the plan back, and the hook replaces that echo with a short pointer to save repeating it. Before doing so it checks that the echoed text really is this call's plan, and that check accepted the plan appearing anywhere inside the text. A plan reading `refactor` is inside almost any paragraph, so an approval message that merely used the word had its whole body replaced by the pointer and the content was lost. The echo starts where the plan starts, so the check is now anchored there: the text must begin with the plan, or be the beginning of it when the echo was cut short. See [src/hooks_exitplanmode.ts](src/hooks_exitplanmode.ts), regression-tested in [tests/hooks_exitplanmode.test.ts](tests/hooks_exitplanmode.test.ts).
- **The cache writer could throw out of a hook, which it promises never to do.** Every cached value passes through one function that writes it to disk and returns false rather than throwing, because it runs inside hooks where a thrown error would break the tool call being made. Turning the value into JSON happened just outside that promise, and turning a value into JSON can itself fail: an object that refers back to itself, or one holding a very large integer, throws on the spot and the error escaped the function. It is now inside the guard with everything else and returns false. See [src/disk_cache.ts](src/disk_cache.ts), regression-tested in [tests/disk_cache.test.ts](tests/disk_cache.test.ts).
- **A trailing comment on the line above a function turned the file's license header, and every line of code in between, into that function's documentation.** Documentation is taken from the comment block immediately above a symbol. When that line ended in `*/` the search walked upwards for the line that opens the block, and it stopped at the first line *starting* with `/*`, which is not the same thing. A line such as `int cached = compute(); /* cached */` ends in `*/` without opening anything, so the search sailed past it into the file, usually as far as the license header at the top, and everything between the two was stored as the function's documentation: source lines, string literals and all. That text is shown by `symbol`, `read` and `brief` and is what semantic search matches on, so a file with a header comment and any trailing comment above a function fed whole passages of unrelated code into both. A `*/` anywhere except the very end of the block now means the lines in between are code rather than comment, and no documentation is taken. Genuine block comments, single-line or multi-line, are unaffected. Confirmed on real files in C and Rust before and after. See [src/doc_comment.ts](src/doc_comment.ts), regression-tested in the new [tests/doc_comment.test.ts](tests/doc_comment.test.ts), which is the first test file this shared helper has had.
- **One stray space after a `=======` line hid a whole merge conflict from `conflicts`.** A conflict is bounded by four marker lines, and three of them were allowed to carry trailing spaces or a branch name after the marker, as git itself writes them. The `=======` in the middle was not: it had to be exactly seven characters and nothing else. A single trailing space, which any editor may leave behind and which several merge tools write, meant the line was read as ordinary content, so the conflict was never reported and the file was instead flagged as reaching the end without a closing `>>>>>>>` when the closing marker was plainly there. Trailing spaces are now allowed, matching the other three markers. Only spaces: unlike those markers, text after the `=======` is still not accepted, because a line of prose beginning with seven equals signs would otherwise be mistaken for the separator and silently cut the conflict short. Eight or more equals signs, as a heading underline is written, are still not a separator either. See [src/conflict_query.ts](src/conflict_query.ts), regression-tested in [tests/conflict_query.test.ts](tests/conflict_query.test.ts).
- **Three faults reading coverage reports, found by an independent review of the parser.** Two functions in one file may share a name, which happens whenever two classes have a method of the same name or a nested function shadows an outer one. LCOV lists each separately, but they were stored under the name alone, so all but the last were thrown away: the file's function total was short by one for each, and the earlier ones could never be reported as untested no matter what the report said. Each listing is now kept on its own, while a genuinely repeated listing of the same function still counts once. Hit counts are still recorded by name, because that is all the format gives, but they are now added up rather than overwritten, so a function that ran is no longer reported as untested because a later line for the same name said zero. Separately, an untested function from an Istanbul report was reported at the line its body opens on rather than the line it is declared on, which differ whenever a function is written across several lines; the declaration line is what the code's own description promised and is the line worth jumping to. And a summary report for a project with nothing instrumented, which contains only its overall total, was reported under the wrong format name, because removing the total left nothing to recognise it by. See [src/coverage_query.ts](src/coverage_query.ts), regression-tested in [tests/coverage_query.test.ts](tests/coverage_query.test.ts).
- **A rebuild briefly left the built program unable to start.** Splitting the program into pieces, below, gave each piece a name derived from its contents, so a build that changes the code writes new names and the previous build's pieces have to be removed. That removal ran first, before the new pieces were written: for the length of the build the starting file from the previous build was still there, still naming pieces that had just been deleted, so anything starting the program in that window failed outright with a missing-module error. The test suite starts the built program about a thousand times, which is enough for a build in another window to land inside it and fail tests that have nothing to do with the change being built. Removal now runs after the build and keeps exactly what that build wrote, so the old pieces stay readable until the new ones exist and the folder is never in a half-finished state. Both halves of the job are now tested directly rather than by checking the folder afterwards, because the suite rebuilds before any test runs and on a fresh checkout that build starts from an empty folder, where such a check passes even with the removal deleted outright. See [scripts/sweep-chunks.mjs](scripts/sweep-chunks.mjs), [esbuild.config.mjs](esbuild.config.mjs) and [tests/guards/core_bundle_stays_split.test.ts](tests/guards/core_bundle_stays_split.test.ts).
- **`worker start` would have reported a background worker it had in fact just killed.** To run in the background the worker starts a second copy of the program and tells it to be a daemon. It found the program to start by asking which file its own code had ended up in, which was the whole program while the program was one file. Splitting it into pieces, above, made that the wrong file: the worker's code now sits in a piece that is a library with no starting point of its own, so the new process loaded it, did nothing and exited, while `worker start` printed the number of a process that was already gone and no indexing ever happened in the background. It now starts the program by name, which does not depend on how the pieces are arranged. This never reached a release, and was caught by the existing end-to-end test that starts a real background worker and waits for it to report in. See [src/worker.ts](src/worker.ts) and [tests/worker_daemon_e2e.test.ts](tests/worker_daemon_e2e.test.ts).
- **The disk caches were never cleaned up on their own, and one of them grew without any limit at all.** Every cached tool output is written through a single function that, having written one file, then removes anything in that folder past its age and count limits. Session state is the exception: it is written directly, not through that function, so nothing ever removed a session file. On this machine that folder held 83044 files and 137 MB, going back months, and every hook that looks at sibling sessions had to read past all of them. The background worker now applies the same age limit to the cache folders on the same hourly round it already uses to rotate its log and clear old snapshots. Sessions are aged out only, never trimmed by count: a session file holds the live state of a conversation and cannot be fetched again, so removing one because there are many would quietly reset a conversation that is still going. Ageing them is safe because a live session rewrites its own file on every hook, so its timestamp never goes stale. Two further things are now cleaned that never were. Anything in a cache folder that is not a `.json` file was skipped outright, so payloads written by older versions, leftovers from an interrupted write, and lock files whose owner had died stayed there for good; they are now aged out with everything else, while the count and size limits still count only the `.json` files they are expressed in. And on Windows these caches used to live under a different folder, which nothing has written to since June and nothing would ever have removed; the sweep covers both folders with the same age limit, so a folder still in use keeps its recent files and a folder no longer in use simply empties. Measured on this machine by starting the worker on the built binary: the session folder went from 83044 files and 137 MB to 409 files and 42 MB, and the old Windows folder from 18593 files and 52 MB to nothing, with the current session's own file untouched and hooks still working afterwards. See [src/disk_cache.ts](src/disk_cache.ts) and [src/worker.ts](src/worker.ts), regression-tested in [tests/disk_cache_sweep.test.ts](tests/disk_cache_sweep.test.ts) and [tests/worker.test.ts](tests/worker.test.ts).
- **Three Apex indexing faults, found by an independent review of the extractor.** A method whose opening brace sits on the next line, which is ordinary formatting, quietly took the following method with it: the search for the end of a parameter list was unbounded and the brace had to share a line with the closing bracket, so the match ran past the first method and swallowed the second one's header. The first method still came out right, which is why nothing looked wrong; the second was simply absent from the index. The parameter list is now bounded to characters that cannot appear in one, so a match can no longer cross from one declaration into another, and a line break before the brace is accepted. Separately, a trigger whose event list wraps across lines, which is how any trigger handling more than one event is written, was not recognised, and the same lines were then read as a method: the file's only symbol was a method named after the object the trigger fires on, which does not exist. And a method was called a constructor whenever its name matched any type declared anywhere in the file, so in `class Outer { class Inner { void Outer() {} } }` the inner method was reported as a constructor of the outer class. A constructor has no return type and a method always has one, so that now decides it. Apex properties written `Type name { get; set; }` are still not indexed, matching the same deliberate line drawn for C# fields. See [src/languages/apex.ts](src/languages/apex.ts), regression-tested in [tests/salesforce_languages.test.ts](tests/salesforce_languages.test.ts).
- **A here-string threw away the rest of a shell script.** `grep -q x <<< "hello"` is an ordinary bash redirect that feeds one word to a command. The extractor's heredoc pattern matched it anyway, starting from the second `<`, and took `hello` for the marker that ends a heredoc body. Every line after it was then treated as text inside that body until a line reading exactly `hello`, which normally never comes: in a real script every function below the here-string was lost. `<<<` is now excluded, and a genuine heredoc still masks its body as before. Two smaller faults are fixed alongside it. A line may open more than one heredoc (`cat <<A <<B`), and only the first marker was remembered, so the second body was read as ordinary code and anything declared inside it indexed as real; all markers on a line are now queued in order. And a function name was allowed only letters, digits and underscore, though bash accepts `-`, `.`, `+` and `:` as well: `my-func()` matched nothing and was dropped, while `function other-func` was silently truncated and stored as `other`, a name nothing would ever search for. See [src/languages/bash_idx.ts](src/languages/bash_idx.ts), regression-tested in [tests/languages.test.ts](tests/languages.test.ts).

### Changed
- **Every hook now starts about 15 ms faster.** A hook fires on nearly every tool call, and the bundle it loads is compiled in full before any of it runs, so anything reachable from it by a plain import is paid for every time whether the hook uses it or not. Two imports were dragging in far more than they asked for. The session-start hook wanted one health check out of the `doctor` command, and taking it that way pulled in `doctor` itself along with everything it uses: the indexer worker, the installer, the TypeScript compiler check, and through those the file-reading, graph and archive command surfaces plus a YAML parser and a compression library. Separately, the shared "this project has nothing indexed" message needed one thirteen-line helper that checks whether a folder is a git repository, and took it from a 78 KB module of text commands. Both now live in small files of their own, so the hook loads the check and the helper without the rest. What a hook compiles drops from 4.17 MB across 228 files to 3.22 MB across 209. Measured on the built hook bundle over fifteen alternating pairs: about 58 ms down to about 43 ms, faster in all fifteen. New guards fail if either import comes back, or if the new files grow a dependency that would undo the split, which nothing else would catch: everything still works, it just quietly gets slower again. See [src/symbol_body_probe.ts](src/symbol_body_probe.ts), [src/walk_mode.ts](src/walk_mode.ts) and [src/doctor_result.ts](src/doctor_result.ts), guarded in [tests/guards/hook_eager_set.test.ts](tests/guards/hook_eager_set.test.ts).
- **Every command now starts about 9 ms faster, without touching what it does.** A hook is served by a single module that pulls in every hook handler, the whole bash filter registry and the HTML text extractor, because it has to have them all registered before any hook runs. The command-line surface imported that module at the top of the file, and Node compiles a module in full before running any of it, so `symbol`, `read` and even `--version` paid to compile the entire hook machinery before doing anything, though only `token-goat hook` ever needs it. The same held for the shell-output compressor, which the `compress` command alone uses. Both are now loaded at the moment the one command that needs them runs. The status line needed only the small stdin reader out of that module, so the reader moved into a file of its own with nothing else in it. What gets compiled on every command drops from 2.70 MB to 1.74 MB. Measured on the built program over twenty-five alternating pairs: `--version` about 88 ms down to about 79 ms, faster in twenty-four of the twenty-five, and a `symbol` call about 99 ms down to about 92 ms, faster in twenty-three. A new guard fails if either import is ever moved back to the top of the file, which nothing else would catch: everything still works, it just quietly gets slower again. See [src/cli.ts](src/cli.ts), [src/stdin_json.ts](src/stdin_json.ts) and [src/relay.ts](src/relay.ts), guarded in [tests/guards/cli_defers_hook_subsystem.test.ts](tests/guards/cli_defers_hook_subsystem.test.ts).
- **Every command and every hook now starts about 7% faster.** The program is one file of 3.6 MB, and Node reads and compiles all of it before running any of it. Parts of it are already written to load only when needed, such as the MCP server, but the bundler had been copying them into that single file anyway, so their code was compiled on every run and only the moment it *ran* was postponed. The program is now split into separate pieces that are read only when something asks for them, the same change already made to the hook bundle. What gets compiled on every run drops from 3.61 MB to 2.83 MB. Measured on the built launcher with the compile cache warm, over fifteen alternating pairs of the same `symbol` call: about 149 ms down to about 139 ms, with the split build faster in thirteen of the fifteen. A new guard reads the built files and fails if the program is ever emitted as one piece again, or if every piece is loaded at startup anyway. See [esbuild.config.mjs](esbuild.config.mjs) and [tests/guards/core_bundle_stays_split.test.ts](tests/guards/core_bundle_stays_split.test.ts).
- **Reindexing no longer reads the whole vector store once per file.** When a file is reindexed its old embeddings are removed first. That removal asked for the vectors belonging to the file with a sub-question ("the ones whose id is in this list"), and the vector store cannot answer a sub-question with a lookup: it read every vector it holds, for every single file, and then kept the few that matched. The ids are now fetched first and each vector removed by its own id, which the store does answer with a direct lookup. Measured on the real index here, 16185 vectors, removing 60 files' vectors went from 152 ms to 23 ms, and the gap grows in step with the size of the index rather than staying fixed. A forced reindex of `src` went from about 8355 ms to about 7915 ms over three alternating builds, the difference being almost exactly the removal cost. The rows removed are unchanged, checked by comparing the full remaining id list from both versions against the same starting database. The sub-question had been chosen to avoid a limit on how many ids one query may name; removing one id at a time never approaches that limit either. See [src/embeddings.ts](src/embeddings.ts), with the statement shape pinned in [tests/embeddings_vector_delete_plan.test.ts](tests/embeddings_vector_delete_plan.test.ts).

## [2.6.30] - 2026-08-16

### Changed
- **Hooks now load about 19 ms faster, on nearly every tool call.** A hook loads `dist/token-goat-hook.mjs`, and Node reads and compiles the whole file before running any of it. That file had grown to 3.6 MB because one line in the skill drift check imported the command-line surface directly, dragging in every command, the argument parser and the MCP server. Two of those were already behind lazy imports, but the bundler had been copying them into the single file anyway, so their code was still compiled on every hook and only their execution was postponed. The drift check now loads the command surface lazily, and the bundle is split into separate pieces that are read only when something actually needs them. What gets compiled on every hook drops from 3.6 MB to 2.3 MB, and loading goes from about 56 ms to about 37 ms, measured on the built file with the compile cache warm. A new guard walks the bundle's real import graph and fails if the command surface ever becomes eagerly loaded again. See [esbuild.config.mjs](esbuild.config.mjs), [src/skill_version_drift.ts](src/skill_version_drift.ts) and [tests/guards/hook_bundle_excludes_cli.test.ts](tests/guards/hook_bundle_excludes_cli.test.ts).
- **Every session now starts about 200 ms sooner.** At the start of a session token-goat checks whether the index holds any oversized symbol body, a leftover from before that size was capped. Nothing could answer that question except reading every symbol in the shared index: 226 MB and 231324 rows here, 229 ms, every single session. The check was written to stop at the first offending row, but on a healthy index there is nothing to stop at, so it always read all of them. The index now keeps a small list of exactly the offending rows, which is empty on a healthy index, so the check is a lookup into an empty list instead of a full read: 229 ms down to under a millisecond, measured on the real index. That list costs 4 KB and no measurable time to maintain, because rows under the cap are skipped without writing anything (measured at -0.2%, within noise, over 40000 real rows). The whole session-start hook went from about 490 ms to about 290 ms, and `token-goat doctor`, which runs the same check, from about 2110 ms to about 1730 ms. See [src/db.ts](src/db.ts) and [src/cli_doctor.ts](src/cli_doctor.ts), with the query plan pinned in [tests/cli_doctor.test.ts](tests/cli_doctor.test.ts).
- **`map --compact` got about three times faster, and every project-scoped query with it.** Each command that reads the shared index has to keep to the current project, and it did that by asking for paths that begin with the project folder, written as a `LIKE` pattern with an escape character. SQLite can normally turn a "begins with" pattern into an index lookup, but it switches that off entirely whenever an escape character is named, which this always did: so both halves of the map query read every row in the machine-wide index and then discarded the other projects. The same test is now written as a plain range, which reads only the current project's rows and needs no escaping at all, since `%` and `_` in a folder name are now ordinary characters. Measured on the built binary against a 231258-symbol, 1111304-reference index, `map --compact` went from about 720 ms to about 230 ms; the reference count within it went from 222 ms to 56 ms and the symbol lookup from 120 ms to 6 ms. The rows selected are unchanged: the old and new filters were compared across 1820 real folder prefixes on all four tables that use them, 7280 comparisons with no difference. On a case-sensitive filesystem there is one deliberate change, because `LIKE` quietly ignored capitalisation: a project at `/x/Repo` no longer matches rows belonging to the genuinely different `/x/repo`. See [src/sql_path.ts](src/sql_path.ts) and [src/baseline.ts](src/baseline.ts), with the query plan pinned in [tests/baseline_top_symbols_plan.test.ts](tests/baseline_top_symbols_plan.test.ts).
- **`dead` got about 20% faster.** Before listing anything, the command checks that the kind of symbol asked for is a real one.
