It did that by reading every distinct kind out of the index, which cannot use an index of its own and so reads the whole shared store: 167 ms of an 846 ms run, measured here. Almost every request names a kind from the short built-in list, and the default kind is one of them, so that list is now checked first and the index is only read when the answer is not already there. The run went from about 846 ms to about 690 ms over three alternating builds, with byte-identical output across twelve kind spellings including the unknown-kind error and its exit code. See [src/graph_commands.ts](src/graph_commands.ts).
- **`refs` on a TypeScript symbol got about 11% faster.** To tell apart two different things that share a name, the command builds a small TypeScript program and asks the compiler which declaration each use points at. Building that program was parsing every documentation comment in every file it pulled in, which this step never looks at: it only ever asks whether two names resolve to the same declaration, and it never reports a compiler error. Documentation comments are now skipped in TypeScript files, and still parsed in plain JavaScript files, where they are the only place a type can be written. A `refs` call measured on the built binary went from about 1180 ms to about 1053 ms, over three alternating builds, with byte-identical output on five symbols. See [src/ts_refs.ts](src/ts_refs.ts).
- **Every command and hook now starts about 20% faster.** Node can cache the compiled form of a large program between runs, but only if that caching is switched on before the program is loaded. The command now starts from a tiny launcher that switches it on and then loads the main program, so the work of compiling 3.5 MB of code is done once and reused. A bare command went from about 131 ms to 108 ms, and a hook call, which happens on nearly every tool use, went from about 145 ms to 112 ms. See [esbuild.config.mjs](esbuild.config.mjs).

### Fixed
- **Nine PowerShell indexing faults, found by an independent review of the extractor.** Four of them lost the rest of the file rather than one symbol, because each left the brace counter stuck above zero and nothing after that looked top-level any more: a quoted string running over several lines was read as code, a backtick-escaped brace such as ``Write-Output `{`` was counted as real nesting, only the first `<# ... #>` comment on a line was removed so the second one ate the closing brace, and a finished comment sitting before a here-string header stopped the here-string from being recognised at all. A declaration written inside a multi-line string was also indexed as if it existed. The other four each lost a single symbol: a method sharing a line with its class header, a method whose return type nested brackets more than two deep, a class or enum carrying an attribute on the same line, and any name with a non-ASCII character, which was silently truncated to its ASCII prefix and stored under that wrong name. See [src/languages/powershell_idx.ts](src/languages/powershell_idx.ts) and [tests/languages.test.ts](tests/languages.test.ts).
- **Lua comments and multi-line strings were read as code, inventing functions and misfiling real ones.** Lua writes block comments and multi-line strings the same way, with `[[` and `]]` brackets, and only the opening line looks like a comment one line at a time. Everything between the brackets was treated as ordinary code, so a commented-out or documented `function` was indexed as if it existed, and its `end` closed a scope that was still open. A second fault had the same effect without any comment involved: a function passed to a call or stored in a table ends on `end)` or `end,`, and only a line holding nothing but `end` was recognised as a close, so those scopes were never closed and every function written afterwards was recorded as living inside one of them. Both are fixed, including bracket levels such as `[==[`, and `[[` inside a quoted string no longer starts a span. See [src/languages/lua.ts](src/languages/lua.ts) and [tests/languages.test.ts](tests/languages.test.ts).
- **Sixteen Swift indexing faults, found by an independent review of the extractor.** Two of them corrupted a whole file rather than one declaration. A regex literal such as `let openBrace = /\{/` is ordinary Swift 5.7, and the brace inside it was counted as real nesting, so the enclosing type never closed and every later declaration in the file was recorded as one of its methods. A nested block comment, which Swift allows, ended at the inner `*/` instead of the outer one, exposing a commented-out `}` that closed the type early and dropped every member after it. Beyond those, declarations were dropped or renamed: a name containing a non-English letter was cut short, so `struct Café` was indexed as `Caf` and its members were filed under that name; a backtick-escaped name such as `` var `default` `` was dropped; a nested generic (`func f<C: Collection<Int>>`) was dropped; `var a = 0, b = 1` recorded only `a`; a type written entirely on one line (`struct S { var value = 0 }`) lost its members; a declaration indented at file scope, as inside an `#if` block, was ignored because indentation was treated as meaning; a failable initializer was stored as `init?`, which nobody would search for, and is now `init`; a file-scope `let` or `var`, which is how Swift writes a global constant, was never indexed at all. Several ordinary modifiers made the extractor miss the whole line: `nonisolated(unsafe)` and `unowned(unsafe)`, `consuming` and `borrowing`, `prefix`/`postfix` on operator functions, and `optional` on an `@objc` protocol requirement. Finally, `import` lines carrying an attribute (`@preconcurrency import Foundation`) or a Swift 6 access level (`public import Core`) were not recorded. That last one had a second cause worth naming: the `imports` command kept its own copy of the extractor's import pattern, so the two drifted apart and the command reported nothing for a file the index held correctly. They now share one pattern. See [src/languages/swift.ts](src/languages/swift.ts), [src/languages/common.ts](src/languages/common.ts) and [src/read_commands.ts](src/read_commands.ts), regression-tested in [tests/languages.test.ts](tests/languages.test.ts) and [tests/read_commands.test.ts](tests/read_commands.test.ts).
- **Elixir documentation was read as code, inventing functions and misplacing real ones.** `@moduledoc` and `@doc` bodies are heredocs, and they almost always contain example code. The extractor read every line of them as ordinary source, so a `def` shown in an example was indexed as a real function that does not exist, and the next real function in the file was recorded as belonging to that invented one. Worse, a bare `end` inside a heredoc, which is normal in an `iex>` example, closed the module as far as the extractor was concerned: every declaration after it was attributed to the wrong module, or to none. The four ways of writing a heredoc are now all skipped over: `"""`, the charlist `'''`, the sigil form `~S"""`, and the one-line form that opens and closes on the same line. A `"""` inside a `#` comment is correctly not treated as an opener. This reuses the same skipping machinery the other languages already share rather than a new one. See [src/languages/elixir.ts](src/languages/elixir.ts) and [src/languages/common.ts](src/languages/common.ts), regression-tested in [tests/languages.test.ts](tests/languages.test.ts).
- **Eight C# indexing faults, found by an independent review of the extractor.** The worst was `#region {`, an ordinary way to label a region right after an opening brace: the brace inside that line was counted as real code, so the enclosing class never closed, its own members were lost, and every later type in the file was recorded as sitting inside it. A `#if false` block was read as live code in the same way, indexing declarations the compiler never sees and leaving its unclosed braces behind. Beyond that, five shapes of member simply never matched and were dropped: a fully-qualified type (`System.Threading.Tasks.Task Run()`, `System.Collections.Generic.List<int> Items`), a tuple return type (`(int a, string b) Pair()`), an explicit interface implementation (`void IDisposable.Dispose()`, now indexed as `Dispose`), a member written at column zero, and a member whose attribute argument contains brackets (`[JsonPropertyName("x[y]")]`). A property written in the Allman style was dropped whenever a comment sat between its name and its `{`, because the search for the accessor block only looked at the next two lines whatever they held. Finally, a lowercase-initial property or type name was rejected outright by four of the patterns: unconventional, but legal. A file exercising all of these went from 2 symbols to 9. Fields, events and constants are still not indexed, which is by design: this extractor covers types, methods, constructors, properties and imports. See [src/languages/csharp.ts](src/languages/csharp.ts), regression-tested in [tests/languages.test.ts](tests/languages.test.ts).
- **`read`, `brief`, `section`, `refs` and `symbol` silently ignored every argument after the first.** Writing `token-goat read a.ts::x b.ts::y` returned only `x` and said nothing about `y`, so a caller could believe it had seen a symbol it never got. This is the likeliest way to get it wrong, because the merged form these commands do support is comma-separated and a space is the habit from every other tool. A note for exactly this already existed and was already printed by `outline`, `skeleton`, `exports` and `imports`; it was simply never wired to the five commands above. It is now, naming the dropped arguments and the comma-separated command that reads them all: `token-goat read "a.ts::x,b.ts::y"`. `symbol` and `section --list` have no merged form, so they say the extras were ignored without suggesting a command that would not work. The first argument is still served exactly as before. Nothing tested this note on any command, which is why the gap was not noticed; all nine are covered now. See [src/cli.ts](src/cli.ts) and [src/read_commands.ts](src/read_commands.ts), regression-tested in [tests/cli_extra_positional_args.test.ts](tests/cli_extra_positional_args.test.ts).
- **Five more Dart indexing faults, found by an independent review of the extractor.** A plain unnamed constructor such as `const A() : value = 0;` was recorded as a *function* named after its own class, so the file held two different symbols both spelled `A`. A field holding a function or an initialising call, such as `final void Function() cb = ...` or `var lazy = compute();`, looked like a method declaration and produced a symbol named `Function` or `compute` that does not exist. A getter written at file scope, `int get version => 1;`, was only ever looked for inside a class and so was never indexed. A generic extension, `extension E<T> on List<T>`, was not recognised at all, which dropped every member declared inside it as well as the extension itself. And `class B = Object with M;`, a valid class declaration with no body, opened a scope that could never close, so the next declaration in the file was attributed to it and lost. A file exercising all five went from 4 symbols to 8. See [src/languages/dart.ts](src/languages/dart.ts), regression-tested in [tests/languages.test.ts](tests/languages.test.ts).
- **Dart constructors and getters were missing from the index.** A named constructor (`A.named()`), a factory constructor (`factory A.create()`) and a getter (`int get value => 1`) were all skipped, so looking any of them up found nothing. Only the one shape with a parameter list and a leading word was picked up, which is why the setter `set value(int v)` was recorded while its matching getter was not: `set` happens to read like a return type. Named and factory constructors are now recorded under the name after the dot, and getters under their own name. The unnamed `A()` form is deliberately still skipped, because it has no name of its own and recording it would clash with the class. A file that previously indexed 4 symbols now indexes 7. See [src/languages/dart.ts](src/languages/dart.ts), regression-tested in [tests/languages.test.ts](tests/languages.test.ts).
- **Lua methods written with a colon were indexed under the wrong name.** `function M:bar()` is the ordinary way to write a method in Lua, and it was stored whole as `M:bar`, so looking it up by its own name found nothing: both `token-goat symbol bar` and `read "file.lua::bar"` missed it. The name was being trimmed at the last dot only, which is why the dotted form `function M.foo()` on the line right above it correctly resolved to `foo`. It is now trimmed at a colon as well, matching what the function-assignment path in the same file already did. See [src/languages/lua.ts](src/languages/lua.ts), regression-tested in [tests/languages.test.ts](tests/languages.test.ts).
- **The new launcher could not start at all on Node 22.0, and broke `require("token-goat")`.** Two problems in the six-line launcher described above. It asked for `enableCompileCache` by name from `node:module`, but that function only exists from Node 22.1 and the package still says it supports 22.0: asking for a name a module does not have is a failure while the file is being linked, before any of its own code runs, so the surrounding "carry on without the cache" guard never got the chance to help and every command and hook would have failed outright. It now reaches the function through the whole module rather than by name, so an older Node simply skips the cache. Separately, the launcher waited for the main program to load, which makes the file an asynchronous module: that file is also what `require("token-goat")` resolves to, so a plain `require` of the package started failing with `ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE`. It no longer waits, and reports a load failure instead. Both were reproduced against the built file before the fix. See [esbuild.config.mjs](esbuild.config.mjs), guarded in [tests/guards/launcher_stays_thin.test.ts](tests/guards/launcher_stays_thin.test.ts).
- **The "everything was filtered out" message contradicted itself when it described a single item.** It correctly said "all 1 type declaration **was** filtered out" and then finished with "widen or drop the filter to see **them**". The closing word now matches the count, so a single item reads "to see it". See [src/util.ts](src/util.ts).
- **`token-goat index <file>` said a tracked file was not tracked.** Pointing the command at a single file instead of a folder always failed with "no tracked files found ... (is it a git repo?)", even when git tracked the file. The lookup asked git to run from the path it was given, and git cannot run from inside a file. It now runs from the file's folder and asks about that one file. See [src/repomap.ts](src/repomap.ts).
- **Throttle marker files piled up in the data folder without limit.** The background indexer writes one small marker per folder it has seen, and nothing ever removed them, so a long-lived install collected hundreds. Markers past their one-hour window are already ignored, so they are now deleted on the indexer's regular cleanup pass. See [src/index_prune.ts](src/index_prune.ts) and [src/worker.ts](src/worker.ts).
- **A file could be dropped from the reindex queue and never picked up again.** When the background indexer recovers a queue file left behind by an earlier crashed run, it first has to read it. If that read failed, the file was immediately set aside as corrupt, which permanently removes it from recovery and deletes it a month later, so every file it named was silently never reindexed. A failed read is not proof of damage: on Windows an antivirus scan or another program holding the file open makes a read fail for a moment and then succeed. The indexer now retries the read a few times before giving up, and still sets the file aside if it really is unreadable. See [src/worker.ts](src/worker.ts).
- **The indexer could skip a batch of queued files it had never actually processed.** To avoid redoing work, it remembers the contents of a queue file it could not delete. It compared only the contents, so a different queue file that happened to hold exactly the same list was mistaken for the one already handled and skipped. That is a likely coincidence rather than a rare one, because editing the same source file again queues the same path again. The record now also notes which file it came from, so only the genuine repeat is skipped. Those records are also cleared once the files they describe are gone, instead of building up in memory for as long as the indexer runs. See [src/worker.ts](src/worker.ts).
- **R's `setMethod("as.data.frame", ...)` was indexed under the wrong, truncated name.** The regex that pulls the method name out of an S4 `setMethod` call stopped at the first dot, so a dotted method name like `as.data.frame` was recorded as just `as`. Looking up the real name found nothing, and the wrong short name showed up in its place. The regex now allows dots in the captured name, matching how `setClass` already handled dotted class names. The same pattern also required the name to be at least two characters long, so a one-letter method such as `setMethod("f", ...)` was skipped altogether rather than recorded wrongly: that is fixed too. See [src/languages/r.ts](src/languages/r.ts), regression-tested in [tests/languages.test.ts](tests/languages.test.ts).
- **`map --compact` took nearly four times longer than it needed to.** Building the project map counts how often each symbol is referenced, and that count was worked out by reading every reference row in the whole index, across every project, and then throwing away the ones belonging to other projects. On a shared index of 751731 references, keeping the 7918 that mattered cost 1754ms of the command's 2330ms. It now reads only the current project's rows. The same query also dragged every symbol's full text through its ranking step before keeping the top handful, so the text is now fetched only for the symbols that actually survive. Together these take the command from 2330ms to 618ms, with byte-identical output. See [src/baseline.ts](src/baseline.ts).
- **Many ordinary ways of using a symbol counted as not using it.** Reference extraction only recognised a name sitting directly in a value position, so anything wrapped around it hid the name: `myHelper as Handler`, `myHelper satisfies T`, `myHelper!`, `<T>myHelper`, `myHelper<T>`, `(myHelper)`, `void myHelper` and `await myHelper` all recorded nothing. Many plain positions had no handling at all: object shorthand `{ myHelper }`, spread in objects and arrays, computed keys `{ [myHelper]: 1 }`, comma expressions, `yield myHelper`, decorators in both TypeScript and Python, and augmented assignment such as `cur ||= myHelper`. On the Python side the same was true of dictionary values, f-string interpolation, tuples and sets, `*` and `**` unpacking, comprehension bodies and the thing a comprehension iterates over, lambda bodies, `await`, `yield` and `raise`. Each one meant a symbol that is genuinely used looked unreferenced, so `refs` found nothing and `dead` called it unused. Exports are still deliberately not counted, because treating `export default myHelper` as a use would make every exported symbol look used and leave `dead` with nothing to report. See [src/parser.ts](src/parser.ts).
- **A test could fail with a file-not-found error that had nothing to do with it.** One test writes a temporary test file into `tests/` and deletes it when it finishes, and several checks walk `tests/` reading every file they find. Running at the same time, a check could list that temporary file and then fail trying to read it after it was already gone. The temporary file now lives in its own ignored directory outside `tests/`, so nothing walking `tests/` can see it. See [tests/retry_visibility_reporter.test.ts](tests/retry_visibility_reporter.test.ts).
- **A base class or class field used from a `.js` file counted as unreferenced.** Reference extraction recognised two class shapes by their TypeScript node names only: a class field, and the base class in an `extends` clause. JavaScript is parsed with a separate grammar that names both differently, so on a `.js` file neither was ever recognised. The effect was that `refs` returned nothing for a base class extended only from JavaScript, and `dead` reported it as unused. Both spellings are now accepted. The reason this went unnoticed is that every existing test for these shapes used a `.ts` file, so the new tests check the JavaScript and TypeScript spellings side by side. See [src/parser.ts](src/parser.ts).
- **`token-goat semantic` credited only 1 byte saved for a workspace-evidence hit, no matter how large the cached text was.** When indexed source has no match, `semantic` falls back to cached workspace evidence and records a stat for the saving. That call passed a literal `0` as the "full source size" instead of the cached text's real size, so `bytesSaved = Math.max(1, 0 - emittedBytes)` always floored to 1: a hit on a 32 KB cached entry recorded the same 1-byte saving as a hit on a 100-byte one. It now sums the actual byte length of the matched entries' cached text, matching how every other `semantic_search` call site already measures its saving. See [src/read_commands.ts](src/read_commands.ts).
- **Every Claude Code hook recompiled the 3.4 MB hook bundle from scratch.** A hook fires on every tool call, and the shim loads that bundle each time. V8 was compiling it from source on every run: about 40 ms of the roughly 148 ms a hook took. The shim now turns on V8's compile cache before it loads the bundle, so the compiled form is reused. That is worth about 23 ms off every tool call, measured twice on the installed shim by running both versions alternately (148 ms against 125 ms, and 186 ms against 163 ms on a busier machine). The call has to sit in the shim rather than in the bundle, because a module is already compiled by the time its own code runs, so a bundle cannot cache itself. If it fails, for example on Node 22.0 where the function does not exist yet, or when the cache directory cannot be written, the shim carries on without the cache rather than failing the tool call. See [src/bridges/claudecode.ts](src/bridges/claudecode.ts).
- **`worker start` ignored `TG_WORKER_POLL_MS`.** The daemon reads that variable to decide how often to drain the dirty queue, but the parent that spawns it wrote the 2000 ms default into the child's environment unconditionally, overwriting whatever it had inherited. So the variable worked only when a caller passed the interval in code, and was inert on the one path that actually starts a daemon. Both ends now go through one shared `resolvePollIntervalMs`, which takes an explicit value first, then the variable, then the default, and ignores an empty, non-numeric, zero, or negative setting rather than polling on it: the parent can no longer forward a value the child would reject and silently swap out. See [src/worker.ts](src/worker.ts).
- **Tests that assert on real bundle output paid ~228 ms of process startup each.** Those tests spawn `node dist/token-goat.mjs <args>` on purpose, so that no injected seam can hide a broken shipping path, and there are hundreds of them. The cost is not the command: measured here, `--version` (which does nothing) takes 259 ms and `todo .` (which does real work) takes 258 ms, so essentially all of it is Node starting and evaluating a 3.3 MB bundle. A new `--batch-serve` mode ([src/batch_serve.ts](src/batch_serve.ts)) serves invocations from one process that has already paid that once, at **3.2 ms per call against 217.8 ms** for a spawn. It stays the real artifact, the real `run(argv)` entry, the real commander parse and the real command implementations -- only the process boundary is shared. Between requests it restores the working directory, restores the environment key by key, resets `process.exitCode`, and clears the module-cache reset registry. Because a cache no reset covers would let one request colour the next, [tests/batch_serve_equivalence.test.ts](tests/batch_serve_equivalence.test.ts) runs ten command shapes both ways and compares stdout, stderr and exit status byte for byte, and separately pins that cwd, environment and a nonzero exit do not leak forward. [tests/text_commands.test.ts](tests/text_commands.test.ts) uses it and went from 30.9 s to 13.1 s; its 43 stdin-carrying calls still spawn for real, since the protocol passes argv, cwd and env but not a stdin stream. `--batch-serve` is intercepted at `argv[2]` exactly as `--worker-daemon` is, and is loaded by dynamic import, so normal CLI startup is unchanged (measured 250 ms, against 259 ms before). **This does not currently make the full suite faster** -- see the note below.
- **Every invocation of the binary loaded the MCP SDK before doing anything.** `token-goat --version` loaded 154 module files and took ~259 ms, of which ~140 ms was `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`, `zod`, `ajv`/`ajv-formats` and `jsonc-parser` -- packages that only the `mcp-serve` command and the two VS Code install commands need. [src/cli.ts](src/cli.ts) already defers the MCP server behind `await import('./mcp_server.js')` and its comment says this keeps the SDK off the startup path, but that only defers token-goat's own module: the shipped bundle is a single file, so esbuild inlines `mcp_server.ts` into it and hoists that module's static `import` of an external package to the top of the bundle, where ESM evaluates it before any code runs. `createMcpServer` is now async and loads the SDK and zod inside itself, and [src/bridges/vscode_install.ts](src/bridges/vscode_install.ts) loads `jsonc-parser` on first use instead of at module scope. Startup went from **154 module file loads to 13**, and a bundle spawn from **259 ms to 120 ms**. This is paid on every hook Claude Code fires on every tool call, not only in tests; in the test suite alone, which spawns the bundle hundreds of times, total test time fell from 802 s to 571 s. Nothing caught it because nothing asserted what startup loads -- the only statement of intent was a comment, and a comment cannot go red -- so [tests/guards/startup_lazy_deps.test.ts](tests/guards/startup_lazy_deps.test.ts) now traces the real artifact's module loads and fails if any of these packages is back on the startup path, or if the load count creeps up at all.
- **`cli.test.ts` spent half its time starting Node, not testing the CLI.** It went from 23.7 s to 10.6 s by routing 68 of its bundle calls through the existing `--batch-serve` mode instead of spawning a fresh process for each, with the test count (103) and the assertion count (279 `expect()` calls) identical before and after. What stayed a real spawn: the four stdin-carrying calls, the streaming `replace` race, and the lock-holder child. The ten subcommand `--help` calls were batched too, once the `process.exit()` bug described in the next entry was fixed, taking the file to 6.0 s. See [tests/cli.test.ts](tests/cli.test.ts).
- **The git-fixture equivalence test flaked on a one-second race.** [tests/helpers/git-repo.ts](tests/helpers/git-repo.ts) builds a template repository once and copies it, and [tests/git_repo_helper.test.ts](tests/git_repo_helper.test.ts) proves a copy is indistinguishable from a repo built the long way by comparing the full on-disk listing, `.git` included. Neither commit pinned a date, so each hashed differently depending on which wall-clock second it landed in, and git stores a commit's loose object at a path derived from that hash. The two listings therefore matched only while both commits fell inside the same second: fine when the file runs alone, not fine under a loaded suite, where it failed with 42 entries on each side and different contents. The fixture commit now has a fixed author and committer date, which makes the whole repository reproducible, and the test pins the resulting commit SHA as a literal rather than merely comparing the two sides -- agreement between them was what the old assertion already had, and it is what passed by luck. With the pin removed the test now fails on every run rather than one in many, confirmed three times each way.
- **Twelve doctor tests each shelled out to PowerShell to enumerate every process on the machine.** `runDoctor` runs every check, and on Windows one of them lists all running processes via `Get-CimInstance Win32_Process` so it can spot duplicate MCP launchers and orphaned Node processes. Profiled here, that one gather is **1.2 s of `runDoctor`'s 1.5 s**, and twelve tests in [tests/cli_doctor.test.ts](tests/cli_doctor.test.ts) called `runDoctor` while testing something else entirely: the config check, the worker check, the ok/warn/fail formatting. Those twelve accounted for 16 s of the file's 18.3 s, against a median test of 4 ms. `runDoctor` and `runDoctorAndExit` now accept an optional process list, and the tests that are not about process health pass an empty one; the file went to **3.4 s**. This did not weaken coverage, it added some: the gather was previously reachable from no test at all -- `checkMcpProcessHealth` had synthetic-row coverage, but nothing asserted that `runDoctor` wires it in -- so there is now one test that deliberately leaves the argument undefined, checks the result appears, and checks a real gather actually returns this process. Both halves were confirmed by mutation, and `token-goat doctor` itself is unchanged: it passes nothing and still gathers for real.
- **Three more test files stopped spawning a process per assertion.** `cli_note.test.ts` went from 4.56 s to 0.73 s, `pack_cli.test.ts` from 2.86 s to 0.61 s, and `runnable_suggestions_e2e.test.ts` from 5.13 s to 1.84 s, all by routing their bundle calls through `--batch-serve`. Test counts (13, 28, 15) and assertion counts (62, 73, 75) are identical before and after; the diff contains no changed `expect()` line at all. What still spawns: the four `pack` calls that feed the command stdin, since the batch protocol passes argv, cwd and env but not a stdin stream. That is also why the remaining candidates were left alone rather than half-converted: `wire_format_contract_matrix.test.ts`, `bash_compress_rewrite.test.ts`, `session_persistence_e2e.test.ts` and `hook_event_harness_matrix.test.ts` all carry stdin payloads, `install_copilot_cli.test.ts` spawns a shim script rather than the bundle, and `cli_limit_validation.test.ts` and `config_commands.test.ts` never spawn the bundle in the first place -- they drive `run()` in-process.
- **`token-goat <subcommand> --help` called the real `process.exit()`.** [src/main.ts](src/main.ts) documents that this binary must set `process.exitCode` and return rather than exiting, so that buffered stdout finishes flushing -- an exit mid-flush can truncate output already written to a pipe. `run()` arranges that by calling commander's `exitOverride()`, but it called it on the program alone, and only after `buildProgram()` had already registered every subcommand. Commander copies the exit callback into a subcommand at the moment that subcommand is *created*, so all of them had already inherited "no callback" and fell through to commander's default, which is `process.exit()`. It is now applied recursively across the whole command tree. The visible symptom was in the tests, where a batched subcommand `--help` took the shared `--batch-serve` server down with it, but the truncation risk was real for anyone piping subcommand help into `head` or `less`. Nothing caught it because the existing coverage either spawned a fresh process, where a real exit is invisible since the process was ending anyway, or exercised only top-level `--help`, the one command that did get the override. [tests/cli_subcommand_help_no_exit.test.ts](tests/cli_subcommand_help_no_exit.test.ts) now asserts it in-process, at three command depths, where an exit is observable, and [tests/batch_serve_equivalence.test.ts](tests/batch_serve_equivalence.test.ts) compares subcommand and nested-subcommand help against a real spawn.
- **Note: the full suite is bound by worker count, not by how much work it does.** Every change above removes real work, and none of them moved the full-suite wall clock, which sat at 140-142 s throughout. The reason is that `maxWorkers` is 4 on Windows while the machine measured here has 26 logical cores: 453 s of test time over 4 workers leaves the suite idle roughly a fifth of the time, so removing work from a file that is not on the binding worker's chain just widens that gap. Raising the worker count on the same machine, changing nothing else, ran the whole suite green in **92 s at 8 workers and 79 s at 12**, against 141 s at 4. That is acted on in the entry below. The per-file wins are still real for anyone running a single file: `text_commands.test.ts` alone is 2.4x faster.
- **Eleven tests built the same throwaway git repository by shelling out to git three times each.** `git init`, `git add`, `git commit` is three process spawns, and [tests/hooks_bash.test.ts](tests/hooks_bash.test.ts) wanted the identical one-committed-file repo eleven times over. A new [tests/helpers/git-repo.ts](tests/helpers/git-repo.ts) builds it once per process and hands out recursive copies, taking that file from 11.17 s to 10.25 s. A copy is not distinguishable from the real thing -- nothing git writes during those three commands records the repository's own absolute path -- and [tests/git_repo_helper.test.ts](tests/git_repo_helper.test.ts) pins that against a control repo built the long way, comparing tree hash, status, branch name, tracked files, and the full on-disk listing including `.git`. The suite does a bare `git init` with no commit in about eighteen other places, and the same treatment was built for those, measured, and thrown away: replacing a *single* spawn with a recursive copy of a `.git` directory is a wash at best on Windows, where that copy is dozens of small files and each one gets scanned. Eight such swaps in `graph_commands.test.ts` cost 0.23 s rather than saving anything, so they were reverted. The win is in amortising the `add` and the `commit`, not in avoiding `git init`.
- **The worker daemon end-to-end test waited 7.3 seconds on fixed sleeps.** It slept 2 s to see the daemon survive, 5 s to see it drain a seeded queue entry, and 300 ms to see it exit -- each sized to the worst case with a margin on top, because a fixed sleep is also the flakiest way to wait: too short and it fails on a slow machine, too long and it still tells you nothing about when the condition became true. Each is now a poll against a deadline, and the test runs in **1.2 s**. It also got stricter in the process. The survival check no longer infers "still alive" from elapsed time; it waits for the daemon to write its own pid into `queue/drain-heartbeat`, which is positive proof it reached the loop on the far side of the argv dispatch the original bug died at. And the drain check now asserts on *how long* the drain took, which is what makes it able to notice `TG_WORKER_POLL_MS` being ignored again. Both were confirmed by reintroducing each bug and watching the matching assertion fail. See [tests/worker_daemon_e2e.test.ts](tests/worker_daemon_e2e.test.ts).
- **Parser tests leaked a temp directory for every assertion that failed.** Each of them built its fixture by hand -- `mkdtempSync` a directory, write one file into it, parse it, assert, then remove the directory -- with the removal written as the last statement of the test body, so a failing assertion threw straight past it and the directory survived the run. The scaffolding was identical in all 49 tests of [tests/parser_languages.test.ts](tests/parser_languages.test.ts) and in five neighbouring files. A new [tests/helpers/parse-fixture.ts](tests/helpers/parse-fixture.ts) replaces it with one call: `parseFixture(fileName, content)` writes the file into a fresh directory and returns its parse result, and cleanup is no longer the caller's problem at all, because it hands out subdirectories of the one per-process root [tests/helpers/temp-config.ts](tests/helpers/temp-config.ts) already removes on exit (and sweeps if a worker is killed first). So a fixture is now cleaned up whether its test passed, failed, or threw. The helper takes the **full file name** rather than an extension, because language detection keys off the whole basename for files like `package.json` and `Makefile`, and a helper that invented its own name would quietly route those cases to a different parser while their assertions still passed. Test and assertion counts are unchanged (395 `it()` blocks, 1240 `expect()` calls, verified before and after); the migration removed 590 lines and added 176. See [tests/languages.test.ts](tests/languages.test.ts), [tests/parser_markdown_fence.test.ts](tests/parser_markdown_fence.test.ts), [tests/sfc_idx.test.ts](tests/sfc_idx.test.ts).
- **Test runs now share one V8 compile cache across the processes they spawn.** The suite starts roughly 975 child processes that each load the 3.3 MB `dist/token-goat.mjs`; a spawn costs a measured 257 ms against 31 ms for a bare `node -e 0`, so most of it is Node's own module machinery rather than token-goat doing work. [tests/setup/build-bundle.ts](tests/setup/build-bundle.ts) now points them all at one `NODE_COMPILE_CACHE` directory, set in `globalSetup` so it is in place before any worker is forked. Measured honestly: an ~11% saving on a bare `--version` spawn, but only ~1.7% end to end, because a real command spends most of its time in SQLite and indexing work that no bytecode cache touches. Kept because it is free and never negative, not because it is a significant win.
- **Scheduled-prompt pressure now uses observed deliveries, not the prompt marker.** Some schedulers repeat a fixed marker such as `[Scheduled prompt #5]`; token-goat now persists a session-local delivery count and warns at the 25th, 100th, and 250th observed delivery. `token-goat stats --methodology` also documents local estimate formulas and explicitly distinguishes them from provider usage or billing data.
- **The Vitest worker count is now derived from the machine instead of fixed per platform.** It was 4 on Windows and 6 elsewhere, and both numbers were hard-won: 6 workers oversubscribed GitHub's 4-vCPU `windows-latest` runner by 50% and pushed ordinary tests past the 30 s bound across three consecutive workflow attempts, and separately consumed 1.34 GB on a developer workstation and timed out browser, snapshot, daemon and type-reference tests. But the same numbers leave a 26-core workstation running the suite on 4 workers, which is what makes it 141 s when its own test time only justifies about 113 s. The rule is now in [tests/setup/max-workers.ts](tests/setup/max-workers.ts): the old value is both the default and the floor, and a machine goes above it only when it has at least 16 cores **and** at least 32 GB, since the documented failure was heap and heap does not scale with cores. Every CI runner shape therefore lands on exactly the value it landed on before -- 4 on `windows-latest`, 6 on `ubuntu-latest` and `macos-latest` -- and [tests/max_workers.test.ts](tests/max_workers.test.ts) pins those three by value so a later change to the formula cannot quietly raise them. Past the bar the result is a flat 12, which is the largest arm actually measured green here (79 s) rather than an extrapolation, and not a per-core expression, because at the smallest machine that clears the bar a `cpus - 2` term could never bind and would only read as though it did.
- **Pre-push no longer runs Windows and WSL full suites concurrently.** Static checks still run in parallel, while the two resource-intensive test suites run sequentially and retain the existing bounded failure tail plus full temporary log. `token-goat doctor` now also read-only audits global Copilot MCP configuration for Chrome DevTools and Playwright `npx` launchers, reporting only counts and the config path, never server bodies or secrets. See [.lefthook-scripts/run-all-checks.sh](.lefthook-scripts/run-all-checks.sh) and [src/cli_doctor.ts](src/cli_doctor.ts).
- **Session guidance and local verification are now isolated.** Continuation and embedded-skill deduplication keys are scoped to the active session, so one session cannot suppress a first-use hint in another. VS Code user-scope install tests now use temporary workspace roots rather than the repository's live `.vscode/mcp.json`, and pre-push retains each noisy check's full log while printing only the final 120 lines for failures. See [src/hooks_session.ts](src/hooks_session.ts), [tests/install_vscode.test.ts](tests/install_vscode.test.ts), and [.lefthook-scripts/run-all-checks.sh](.lefthook-scripts/run-all-checks.sh).
- **Test-run pressure advice now preserves existing compression.** Commands the Bash compressor can wrap retain its enforced timeout; the advisory is used only when that bounded execution path is unavailable.
- **Scheduled-prompt loops and unbounded test runs now receive bounded advice before they compound context or runtime cost.** At scheduled prompt #25, #100, and #250, the user-prompt hook gives a one-time checkpoint/fresh-session reminder and explicitly notes it cannot recover already-injected tokens. The Bash hook now flags direct test commands with neither a focused selector nor an explicit timeout, without rewriting or stopping the command. See [src/hooks_session.ts](src/hooks_session.ts) and [src/hooks_bash.ts](src/hooks_bash.ts).
- **Semantic search now falls back to bounded workspace evidence after indexed source misses.** `token-goat semantic` embeds at most 100 recent, project-scoped, secret-redacted evidence entries on demand and caches their vectors locally. Results are explicitly labeled `workspace-evidence`, so historical cached material is never presented as live source. Existing Bash, read-only MCP, and prompt-specific WebFetch caches already provide safe output reuse with their original fingerprint, TTL, and provenance checks. See [src/evidence_cache.ts](src/evidence_cache.ts) and [src/read_commands.ts](src/read_commands.ts).
- **Long Copilot sessions now receive bounded checkpoint and duplicate-payload guidance.** A first `continue`/`resume` prompt receives a one-time reminder to checkpoint and restart when older context is no longer needed. Replaying an identical embedded `<skill-context>` body now receives an advisory that it is already loaded, covering a path that bypasses native Skill hook deduplication. Windows `token-goat doctor` also reports duplicate Chrome DevTools/Playwright MCP launchers and orphaned Node processes without terminating host-managed processes. See [src/hooks_session.ts](src/hooks_session.ts) and [src/cli_doctor.ts](src/cli_doctor.ts).
- **Cross-session file-read dedup now has exact evidence verification and startup change capsules.** When `hints.cross_session_read_dedup` is enabled, successful file reads are stored in a bounded, project-scoped cache with SHA-256 verification and secret-redacted bodies. A later read receives an advisory only when the same path's current content matches exactly; changed or missing files are listed at session start for a fresh surgical read, without injecting cached source. See [src/evidence_cache.ts](src/evidence_cache.ts), [src/hooks_read.ts](src/hooks_read.ts), and [src/hooks_session_start.ts](src/hooks_session_start.ts).
- **Re-reading changed source/style/data files now serves a compact diff by default, not the full file.** The existing snapshot pipeline already supported `.ts`/`.css`/`.json`/etc. behind `hints.serve_diff_on_reread`; the default left that high-value path off. It is now enabled by default and remains opt-out via `serve_diff_on_reread = false`.
- **A throwing hook handler no longer prevents later handlers from serving their valid response.** The registry now isolates each handler failure and continues dispatching, preserving the relay and Copilot shim's existing fail-open protection against tool lockouts.
- **The VS Code extension no longer sends an unrecoverable compressed payload when no MCP decoder is available.** It falls back to the PII-scrubbed original text and omits the decoder instruction; a configured or extension-provided decoder still uses compression.
- **`webfetch.allow`/`webfetch.deny` were parsed, validated, and echoed by `token-goat config get`, but no code ever consulted them, so setting a deny list silently did nothing to block a fetch.** `webfetch.max_file_count`/`webfetch.max_bytes` were already wired (they bound the on-disk web-output cache in [src/disk_cache.ts](src/disk_cache.ts)), which made `allow`/`deny` easy to miss as dead alongside working siblings in the same config block. `preFetchHandler` now checks every `WebFetch` call's URL against both lists before the existing dedup/caching logic runs: a URL matching any `deny` pattern is blocked, and when `allow` is non-empty a URL matching none of its patterns is blocked. Patterns are wildcard strings (`*` matches any run of characters, case-insensitive) matched against the full URL -- deliberately not `pack.ts`'s minimatch-based path-glob semantics, since those treat `/` as a segment boundary a bare `*` won't cross, which breaks a pattern like `*.example.com*` spanning a URL's `://` and path segments. A `?` in a pattern is treated as a literal query-string character rather than a regex quantifier: unescaped it made `*example.com/?debug=1*` miss the URL it was written for and match `https://example.com/debug=1` instead, which is the same silently-not-blocking failure this wiring exists to remove. Both lists default to empty, so existing behavior (no blocking) is unchanged. See [src/hooks_fetch.ts](src/hooks_fetch.ts), [src/config.ts](src/config.ts), [tests/hooks_fetch.test.ts](tests/hooks_fetch.test.ts).

## [2.6.29] - 2026-08-13

### Security
- **`changed` accepted a git ref beginning with `-`, turning `git diff` into an arbitrary-file-write primitive.** The ref is placed in argv where git expects a revision, but git's own parser still reads a leading `-` there as an option, so `ref = "--output=<path>"` made git write the diff to that path and truncate whatever was there. Reproduced directly: a file containing a sentinel string came back holding the diff instead. It was reachable over MCP, where the `changed` tool declared `ref` as a bare optional string, and it never passed through the read-confinement gate. `runGit`'s existing `--no-ext-diff`/`--no-textconv` hardening does not cover this -- those close the diff-driver command-execution vector, not option injection. Any ref starting with `-` is now refused; git's own refname rules forbid that shape, so nothing legitimate is lost. See [src/read_commands.ts](src/read_commands.ts), [tests/mcp_server.test.ts](tests/mcp_server.test.ts).
- **New `mcp.allowed_roots` pins which roots an MCP caller may name.** `mcp.confine_reads_to_project_root` stops a caller traversing out of the root it is given, but it never constrained which root the caller supplies: every tool takes an optional `projectRoot`, and MCP tool arguments are model-generated, so that choice is untrusted input. The setting is a list of roots (env `TOKEN_GOAT_MCP_ALLOWED_ROOTS`, delimiter-separated like `PATH`); a resolved root outside every entry is refused. It is **empty by default, so existing behaviour is unchanged** -- `projectRoot` exists precisely because an MCP server's cwd is often not the workspace root, and that contract still holds. The allowlist is read from the server's own config rather than the request's resolved root, deliberately inverting how the sibling confinement flag is scoped: a workspace may decide its own confinement, but must not be able to ship a project config that authorises itself past the operator's allowlist. See [src/mcp_server.ts](src/mcp_server.ts), [src/config.ts](src/config.ts), [src/env.ts](src/env.ts), [tests/mcp_server_allowed_roots.test.ts](tests/mcp_server_allowed_roots.test.ts).
- **Pinned `actions/checkout` and `actions/setup-node` to commit SHAs in the publish workflow.** They were mutable major tags in the one job holding `NPM_TOKEN` and `id-token: write`, so a tag repoint would have run inside the job that publishes to npm under the project's provenance attestation. Pinned at their current v4 commits, matching the existing SHA-pinned `nick-fields/retry` in CI; deliberately not bumped to v7, which would be a behaviour change rather than a security fix. See [.github/workflows/publish.yml](.github/workflows/publish.yml).

### Added
- **The fifteen single-format document readers are now routed to agents instead of being left for a human to memorise.** `pdf-meta`/`pdf-outline`/`pdf-extract`, `docx-outline`/`docx-text`, `pptx-outline`/`pptx-slide`/`pptx-notes`/`pptx-text`, and `xlsx-sheets`/`xlsx-head`/`xlsx-range`/`xlsx-query` were all present but absent from the installed guidance block, so an agent had to already know they existed. They now appear in the agent instructions with an inspect-then-read flow per format, and the PDF read hint points at `pdf-meta`/`pdf-outline` before `pdf-extract --pages` rather than sending the agent straight at whole-file extraction. The guidance coverage guard previously listed all fifteen as deliberate omissions; those exemptions are removed, so the guard now requires each to stay documented. See [README.md](README.md), [src/bridges/guidance_block.ts](src/bridges/guidance_block.ts), [src/hints/file_type_handler.ts](src/hints/file_type_handler.ts), [tests/guards/guidance_body_command_coverage.test.ts](tests/guards/guidance_body_command_coverage.test.ts).
- **`impact --grep` narrows the impacted-set output to entries whose symbol name (or `(module scope) <file>` key) matches a pattern**, closing the one gap left in this flag family after `call-chain`/`callers`/`dead` already had it. Applied before the `--top` slice, so it selects from the whole impacted set rather than an already-capped page; when it matches none of the impacted entries that do exist, the output names how many were filtered out instead of reading as genuinely impact-free. Under `--json` that count goes to stderr: `impact --json` is a deliberate bare array rather than an envelope, so unlike its six grep-capable siblings it has no payload key to carry a `hiddenByGrep`, and wrapping it to hold one would break every existing consumer. Putting the count on the other stream keeps stdout the shape callers already parse while still distinguishing "the filter hid everything" from a genuinely impact-free symbol -- the same "filtered store renders as populated" trap already closed for `dead`/`deps`/`types`/`callers`/`call-chain`. See [src/graph_commands.ts](src/graph_commands.ts), [src/cli.ts](src/cli.ts), [tests/graph_commands.test.ts](tests/graph_commands.test.ts).

## [2.6.28] - 2026-08-13

### Added
- **Image shrink now caches its re-encode on disk, keyed by source path + size + mtime, so a repeat Read of an unchanged image skips the `sharp` re-encode entirely.** Ported from an archived, never-merged change. Cache entries live under `<home>/image_shrink_cache`, are bounded by a `DEFAULT_MAX_AGE_MS`-based sweep run (throttled to once per 60s) on every qualifying image Read, and are scoped to their own `token-goat-shrink-` filename prefix in their own dedicated subdir, so pruning can never touch anything else -- the archived version wrote to the unbounded OS temp dir with no pruning at all, which this deliberately does not carry over. mtime is part of the cache key (not just path + size) so a content change that happens to preserve the exact byte length -- e.g. regenerating a same-dimension screenshot -- still busts the cache. A corrupt or truncated cache entry is detected by re-probing it with `sharp` before it is ever served, deleted, and treated as a miss. A cache hit runs through the same accounting path as a fresh shrink, so `image_shrink` stats stay honest either way. Also adds `.avif`, `.heic`, and `.heif` to the recognised image extensions. See [src/image_shrink.ts](src/image_shrink.ts), [tests/image_shrink.test.ts](tests/image_shrink.test.ts).

### Fixed
- **A confined MCP `grep` could still be walked out of the project root, by repointing what a symlink already resolved to rather than the symlink itself.** The recursive walk boundary-checked each symlink entry once and then recursed into the resolved realpath, but the recursion trusted the directory it was handed and re-checked only its own visited-set, never the boundary. Because that recursive step re-resolves the path string (no pinned descriptor exists to carry the identity across), swapping the resolved target for a link pointing outside the root in that window made the walk enumerate the out-of-root directory and return its contents under an in-root path. The earlier fix closed the variant where the *link* is repointed, which the walk never dereferences again; this closes the variant where its *target* is. The boundary is now re-checked on every recursive entry rather than once at the caller, and the code comment no longer claims the whole class is closed -- the remaining `statSync` window is stated explicitly, along with the no-concurrent-writer threat model it is accepted under. See [src/read_commands.ts](src/read_commands.ts), [tests/mcp_server_read_confinement.test.ts](tests/mcp_server_read_confinement.test.ts).
- **`callers`, `impact`, `call-chain`, `dead`, and `types` had the same "--json" gap for `--exclude-tests` that `hiddenByGrep` had already closed for `--grep`.** When `--exclude-tests` hid every remaining result, `callers --json` and `impact --json` fell straight through to the plain-text stderr message ("No non-test references found for '...' (1 in test file hidden by --exclude-tests)"), skipping the JSON envelope entirely, so a `--json` consumer that read stdout got unparseable prose instead of a body it could parse. `dead --json`, `types --json`, and `call-chain --json` already emitted valid JSON in this case, but with no marker distinguishing "the filter hid everything" from "the store is genuinely empty" -- the same distinction `hiddenByGrep` already exists to make. All five now carry `hiddenByExcludeTests` (the field `brief --json` already used for exactly this), for both the fully-emptied and partially-filtered case, omitted entirely when the flag is absent or hid nothing so default payloads stay byte-identical; `callers`/`impact`'s exit code is unchanged (still 1 for the fully-emptied case) so existing text-mode assertions keep passing. See [src/graph_commands.ts](src/graph_commands.ts), [tests/graph_commands.test.ts](tests/graph_commands.test.ts).
- **`call-chain --grep`, and five sibling commands, emitted a `--json` payload that could not tell "the filter matched none of what exists" from "there was nothing to begin with".** The text paths already say so in prose (`grepFilteredToEmptyNotice`), but the JSON envelopes carried no marker at all: `call-chain --json` emitted a bare `{ chains: [] }`, `refs`/`callers`/`dead`/`types` emitted `{ items: [], truncated: false, totalCount: 0 }`, and `deps` emitted two empty arrays -- byte-identical in both situations, so a machine consumer had no way to distinguish a narrowed view from an empty store. This is the same empty-vs-filtered rendering trap already closed for those commands' human output. All six now carry `hiddenByGrep`, the field `brief --json` already used for exactly this, omitted entirely when the filter is absent or hid nothing so default payloads stay byte-identical. It is emitted for a partially filtered page too, not only a fully emptied one, so the count means the same thing everywhere. See [src/graph_commands.ts](src/graph_commands.ts), [src/read_commands.ts](src/read_commands.ts), [tests/json_envelope_shape.test.ts](tests/json_envelope_shape.test.ts).
- **The VS Code extension's real-PATH entrypoint test failed on macOS because it compared two spellings of the same directory.** The test put its `mkdtemp` directory on `PATH` as `/var/folders/...` but `resolveTokenGoatEntrypoint` returns the resolved `/private/var/folders/...`, so the comparison never matched even though the lookup was correct. Fixed by realpath-ing the temp directory once at creation, so `PATH` and the expected value share one spelling. See [vscode-extension/tests/security.test.ts](vscode-extension/tests/security.test.ts).
- **`vscode-extension`'s shim-path parser and two of its test suites carried Windows-only assumptions that only ubuntu and macOS CI runners exposed, since they never fail on the Windows runner where the underlying code paths naturally already behave correctly.** `parseShimScriptPath` normalized an npm/pnpm/yarn `.cmd` shim's extracted script path with the host platform's default `path` module (`path.normalize`/`path.sep`), even though `.cmd` shims and their `%dp0%`/`%~dp0` tokens are Windows-only syntax with always-backslash-separated paths; on a POSIX host `path.sep` is `/` and `path.normalize` does not collapse the backslash `..` segments in the resolved text, so a POSIX-run parse of a real npm/pnpm/yarn shim silently produced a subtly wrong path (a stray leftover `/` from the substitution, or an uncollapsed `\..\`) instead of the correct one -- not a shipped product defect, since production only ever calls this function on `process.platform === 'win32'` where the host's default `path` module already is `path.win32`, but a latent correctness gap the tests surfaced the moment they ran on a non-Windows host. Fixed by resolving with `path.win32` explicitly, so the function's correctness no longer depends on which host it runs on and the tests exercise the parser directly on every CI platform. Separately, `resolveTokenGoatEntrypoint`'s "not on PATH" test asserted `/Could not find token-goat/`, a regex that only matched by coincidence against the win32 branch's wording ("Could not find token-goat.cmd on PATH") and not the POSIX branch's deliberately different wording ("Could not find the token-goat executable on PATH"); broadened to `/Could not find.*token-goat.*on PATH/` so it asserts the shared substance on both branches rather than one branch's exact phrasing. Separately again, `tests/install_vscode.test.ts` isolated only `APPDATA` between tests, which is the only env var `vscodeUserConfigDir` consults on win32 -- on POSIX it derives the user-scope config path from `os.homedir()` (`HOME`, with `USERPROFILE` as `os.homedir`'s own win32 fallback), so a POSIX CI run left every test in the file writing into the real CI-runner home directory, where an earlier test's `token-goat` VS Code registration persisted and made later tests in the same file see stale "already registered" errors or a false "configured: true". Fixed by isolating `HOME` and `USERPROFILE` alongside `APPDATA` for every case in that file. All three were real, previously-silent defects reachable only from a POSIX CI run; none were reachable in local Windows development. See [vscode-extension/src/launcher.ts](vscode-extension/src/launcher.ts), [vscode-extension/tests/security.test.ts](vscode-extension/tests/security.test.ts), [tests/install_vscode.test.ts](tests/install_vscode.test.ts).
- **The confinement swap-timing tests' own path comparison silently never matched on a Windows runner whose `%TEMP%` is pinned to an 8.3 short name, or on macOS where `os.tmpdir()` returns the `/var` alias, so the swap those tests exist to exercise never fired and they passed vacuously instead of testing anything -- production confinement itself was never broken.** `checkWithinProjectRoot` passes `path.resolve(root, normalizePath(target))` to `fs.realpathSync.native`, and `normalizePath` already expands a short-name segment (via its own `fs.realpathSync.native` call) and rewrites `/var` to `/private/var` before that -- so the string production hands to the spy is already long-form/de-aliased. The tests' `samePath` helper compared that already-normalized string against the literal, still-short/aliased test fixture path using only `path.resolve` plus a case fold, which knows about neither transform, so the two never matched: `expect(swapped).toBe(true)` failed with `swapped` still `false` on every CI run on Windows and macOS specifically (not Linux, which has neither alias), while the read/section/grep/reindex calls under test were actually refused correctly the whole time. Fixed by comparing against a key produced by the app's own `normalizePath`, computed once outside the spy (calling it from inside the spy would recurse into the very `fs.realpathSync.native` call being mocked, through `normalizePath`'s own short-name expansion). Confirmed the failure mode directly against a real Windows 8.3 short-name directory before and after the fix. See [tests/mcp_server_read_confinement.test.ts](tests/mcp_server_read_confinement.test.ts).
- **A nested symlink found by a confined recursive `grep` could still be repointed outside the project root between the moment its realpath was checked and the moment it was actually walked/read.** `searchDir` lstat'd every entry, and for a symlink resolved its realpath and confirmed it fell inside the search boundary -- but then fell through to a separate `fs.statSync`/recursion on the same *pathname*, so the check and the use named two different things and an attacker had a window in between to repoint the link. Fixed by resolving each symlink entry exactly once with `fs.realpathSync`, boundary-checking that realpath, and then stat'ing, recursing into, and reading the **realpath only** -- the link pathname is never referenced again, so repointing it afterwards cannot redirect the walk. The confined walk also tracks the realpaths of directories it has already entered, so a symlink that resolves back into the walked tree neither loops forever nor reports the same file twice. An earlier version of this fix skipped symlink entries outright under confinement; that closed the window but silently cost a real capability (an in-root file reachable only through a legitimate in-root symlink became invisible to confined `grep`), and the realpath-traversal shape closes the same window without that loss. Confinement-only: unconfined CLI `grep` keeps following the symlink pathname exactly as before, since there is no attacker in that model. See [src/read_commands.ts](src/read_commands.ts), [tests/mcp_server_read_confinement.test.ts](tests/mcp_server_read_confinement.test.ts), [tests/read_commands.test.ts](tests/read_commands.test.ts).
- **`symbol`'s nested-JSON/YAML-key miss hint could suggest a `json-query`/`yaml-query` command that does not select the key it just found.** The hint builds a dot-path like `a.b` from the key names on the way to a match, but a key that itself contains `.`, `[`, or `]` is ambiguous in that same dot-path grammar (`parseJsonPath` treats `.` as a path separator and `[`/`]` as a bracket-expression delimiter), so the suggested command would either fail to parse or silently select a different value than the one actually found. Fixed by suppressing the suggestion when a match is reachable only through such a key, rather than trying to escape it into the grammar -- the search keeps looking past an unrepresentable key for another, encodable match at the same name instead of stopping there. See [src/read_commands.ts](src/read_commands.ts), [tests/guards/structured_data_discoverability.test.ts](tests/guards/structured_data_discoverability.test.ts).
- **An in-root path that did not exist yet at MCP confinement-gate validation time got no identity pin at all, and every pin-aware read helper read that missing pin as "confinement is off" rather than "confined but unpinnable."** `checkWithinProjectRoot` stats the target to capture a `dev:ino` identity to pin; a target that cannot be stat'd (because it is genuinely absent) yields no identity, which is correct -- a spec naming a not-yet-created file must still fail as an ordinary "could not read" rather than a confinement refusal. But `confineTargets` then simply skipped recording anything for that path, so the pin map had no entry for it at all, and `readFileText`, `readFileBytes`, `indexFileSyncPinned`, and `runGrep`'s directory checks all treat a missing map entry as "this path was never gated" and fall through to a raw, unverified read -- the exact same code path taken when confinement is disabled entirely. An attacker who names an in-root path that does not exist yet, waits for the gate to validate it as absent-but-in-root, then creates an out-of-root symlink there before the read actually runs, got the swapped file's contents served straight through `read`, `section`, and `grep` alike. Fixed with a negative pin: `confineTargets` now always records an entry for a validated target, using the real identity when one exists or a new `ABSENT_PIN` sentinel when it does not, so "no entry for this path" can no longer be misread as "unconfined" while confinement is active. Every pin-aware read helper now checks for `ABSENT_PIN` first and, via a new `verifyStillAbsent`, refuses (`ConfinementIdentityError`) if something now exists at that path, or falls through to the pre-existing ordinary missing-file behavior if it is still genuinely absent. See [src/mcp_server.ts](src/mcp_server.ts), [src/read_commands.ts](src/read_commands.ts), [tests/mcp_server_read_confinement.test.ts](tests/mcp_server_read_confinement.test.ts).
- **`section` reads bypassed the MCP confinement pin entirely, and `grep`'s directory boundary check had a second, narrower TOCTOU window than the one already fixed.** `section_reader.ts`'s `readTextForSections` (used by `readSection`, `findContainingSection`, and `listSections`) called `fs.readFileSync` directly and never consulted `activePins`, so an in-root file validated by the MCP confinement gate but swapped for an out-of-root symlink before the read still had its replacement's contents returned by `section` (and by `brief`'s section lookup) -- the same class of gap `read` had already been fixed for. `readTextForSections` and the three functions built on it now accept an optional pin-aware reader function, and `runSection`/`runBrief` in `read_commands.ts` pass the existing pin-aware `readFileText` so a swap is now caught the same way it already was for `read`. Separately, `grep`'s top-level search-directory check verified its pin once (`verifyPinnedIdentity`, an fd-based fstat-identity check) and then separately re-resolved the search boundary with a fresh `fs.realpathSync` by pathname -- a swap landing in the gap between those two calls could still put an attacker-controlled directory into the search boundary undetected. This is **narrowed, not closed**: the pin is now re-verified a second time immediately after the boundary is derived, and a `realpathSync` failure on a pinned path now refuses instead of falling back to an unverified `path.resolve`, but no portable (Windows/macOS/Linux) API exists to make the check-then-resolve sequence atomic, so a swap landing in the smaller residual gap between that second verification and the directory walk's first entry read is still possible and undetected. See [src/section_reader.ts](src/section_reader.ts), [src/read_commands.ts](src/read_commands.ts), [tests/mcp_server_read_confinement.test.ts](tests/mcp_server_read_confinement.test.ts), [tests/read_commands.test.ts](tests/read_commands.test.ts).
- **Three follow-on confinement bypasses left over from the previous pinned-read fix, all in the same file.** MCP `grep`'s top-level search directory ignored the confinement gate's identity pin entirely and re-derived its search boundary from a fresh, unverified `fs.realpathSync` -- a directory swapped to an out-of-root symlink in the window between validation and the search was silently accepted as the new boundary, and the recursive walk returned its contents. The pinned reindex helper (`indexFileSyncPinned`, used by `--force-refresh` and stale-index self-healing) fell back to a raw, unpinned `indexFileSync` read whenever the pinned open failed for any reason other than a detected identity mismatch, including an ordinary non-`ENOENT` open failure -- letting a caller who could make the first open fail get an unverified raw read served anyway. And `healStaleIndex`'s best-effort error handling swallowed a detected identity mismatch (`ConfinementIdentityError`) along with ordinary parse/I/O errors, turning a caught swap into silent best-effort behavior instead of a refusal. `grep`'s top-level directory now verifies its pin (open + fstat identity check) before deriving a search boundary from it; `indexFileSyncPinned` now only falls back cleanly on `ENOENT` and refuses (rather than silently reading) on any other open failure; and `healStaleIndex` rethrows `ConfinementIdentityError` instead of catching it. See [src/read_commands.ts](src/read_commands.ts), [tests/mcp_server_read_confinement.test.ts](tests/mcp_server_read_confinement.test.ts).
- **The VS Code extension could not be packaged into a VSIX at all.** `vsce` supports two mutually exclusive ways of choosing what goes into the package -- a `files` allowlist in `package.json`, or a `.vscodeignore` denylist -- and given both it refuses to package rather than merging or preferring one. `files` had been there since the extension was introduced, and a later change added a `.vscodeignore` beside it, so `vsce package` began failing outright. Nothing caught it: lint, all four typechecks and all three test suites stayed green, because none of them packages the extension. The `.vscodeignore` is removed and the `files` allowlist kept, which is the stricter of the two -- under a denylist a new file dropped at the extension root ships by default, under an allowlist it does not. A new guard test asserts exactly one strategy is declared. Note that `vsce ls` accepts the broken combination and exits 0, so listing the files that would ship is not a check for this. See [vscode-extension/tests/packaging.test.ts](vscode-extension/tests/packaging.test.ts).

### Changed
- **The VS Code extension now supplies the chat decoder itself, so there is nothing left to set up.** A compressed payload is only readable by the chat model if it can call the `retrieve_text` MCP tool, and until now arranging that was three manual steps the extension could only nag about: run `token-goat install --vscode`, reload the window, then start the server by hand. The extension now contributes the MCP server through VS Code's `mcpServerDefinitionProviders` contribution point, so VS Code starts `token-goat mcp-serve` on demand the first time the model needs to decode something -- no `mcp.json` is written, no reload, and the setup prompt never appears. Chat still has to be in Agent mode, which no amount of configuration can substitute for. This requires VS Code 1.101 or newer, so the extension's `engines.vscode` moves from `^1.90.0` to `^1.101.0`; the old `mcp-status` check and its install prompt remain as the fallback for anywhere the contribution does not take effect, and `install --vscode` is unchanged for people who do not use the extension. See [vscode-extension/src/extension.ts](vscode-extension/src/extension.ts), [vscode-extension/package.json](vscode-extension/package.json).
- **Compressed payloads sent to chat are now fenced.** Every composer wraps the payload in a sentence of its own and the handoff appends a decoding hint, so the payload previously ran straight into prose on both sides and the model had to guess where it ended. It is now delimited by a fence sized to the payload's own longest backtick run. Nothing `compress-text` emits today contains a backtick -- it is fixed headers plus, at most, a `deflate-raw-base64url` body, and when compression is not a net win the body is withheld rather than emitted raw -- so the self-sizing is defensive rather than currently load-bearing: a fence closed early by its own content truncates the payload silently, with no error at any layer, and the payload format is not frozen. The `recovery: token-goat retrieve <id>` line the model is told to key on is unchanged inside the fence. See [vscode-extension/src/extension.ts](vscode-extension/src/extension.ts).
- **The chat participant now shows progress and its own icon.** Compressing shells out to the CLI and can read a whole document first, so the panel used to sit blank for the entire round trip with no sign anything was happening. See [vscode-extension/src/extension.ts](vscode-extension/src/extension.ts).

### Documentation
- **The README now documents secret redaction, which was a real feature nobody could discover.** Everything token-goat writes to its caches -- Bash and Task output (including the command string, where an inline `--token=...` would otherwise land), fetched web pages, MCP results and labels, `compress-text`/`handoff` payloads, and the raw JSON disk cache -- is passed through a redactor that replaces recognized credentials with a `[REDACTED:<kind>]` marker. It is unconditional and covers fifteen pattern families. The README mentioned it only in passing, as a subordinate clause about handoff storage, and the "Security, privacy, and uninstall" section -- where a reader would actually look -- did not mention it at all. Someone evaluating the tool would reasonably have assumed a `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer ..."` landed in a cache in plain text. The new text also states the two limits plainly: it matches known shapes rather than classifying, so an unrecognized token format is cached as-is, and it protects what token-goat stores rather than what the model already saw. See [README.md](README.md), [src/secret_redact.ts](src/secret_redact.ts).

### Added
- **New `mcp-status` CLI command, and the VS Code extension now checks it instead of reading `.vscode/mcp.json` directly.** `install --vscode` defaults to user scope, so a correctly-installed user has no workspace `mcp.json` at all -- the extension's decoder-setup prompt fired every session for a user who had already run the install successfully, telling them to run the exact command they already ran. `mcp-status --vscode` shares one path resolver (`vscodeDecoderConfigured` in [src/bridges/vscode_install.ts](src/bridges/vscode_install.ts)) with `install`/`uninstall`, so the reader and the writer can never drift on where `mcp.json` lives or what key name it looks for; `--project` also checks the workspace scope. The extension now also runs this check with no workspace folder open, since a user-scope install is workspace-independent and was previously undetectable in that case. See [src/cli.ts](src/cli.ts), [vscode-extension/src/extension.ts](vscode-extension/src/extension.ts), [tests/install_vscode.test.ts](tests/install_vscode.test.ts), [vscode-extension/tests/decoder_setup.test.ts](vscode-extension/tests/decoder_setup.test.ts).
- **`section --list` now takes `--grep <pattern>` to filter the headings it prints, matching the `--grep` semantics already used by `outline`/`skeleton`/`types`/`exports`/`imports`/`deps` (a regex, falling back to a literal substring match if the pattern doesn't compile).** A pattern that matches nothing is distinguished from a file that genuinely has no headings: matching none of a non-empty heading list reports a "filtered out by --grep" notice and exits 0 with a well-formed empty `--json` envelope (`{items: [], truncated: false, totalCount: 0}`), while a file with no headings at all keeps the pre-existing "No sections found" wording and exit code, even if `--grep` was also passed. See [src/read_commands.ts](src/read_commands.ts), [src/cli.ts](src/cli.ts), [tests/cli_section_list.test.ts](tests/cli_section_list.test.ts).
- **New `image-meta`/`image-text` commands mirror the `pdf-*` family for images.** `image-meta` reads dimensions, format, and byte size via `sharp` metadata only -- a cheap "should I even look at this" probe that never runs OCR -- and reports what a `shrinkImage` pass would cost. `image-text` runs OCR through the existing isolated-subprocess `ocrImage` and is honest about weak results: confidence and character count are always reported, and text below `isTextHeavy`'s usefulness threshold is withheld as noise instead of printed as content. Each command depends on its own optional dependency independently (`sharp` for `image-meta`, `tesseract.js` for `image-text`), so one missing dep never breaks the other, and each degrades with a clear, actionable message rather than crashing. Both take `--json` and reject a non-image file or nonexistent path the same way the `pdf-*` family does. See [src/read_commands.ts](src/read_commands.ts), [src/image_shrink.ts](src/image_shrink.ts), [src/cli.ts](src/cli.ts).
- **The guidance block now has a failure-shape row for reading the text in an image, not just for checking its dimensions.** The row added alongside `image-meta` covered inspecting an image's dimensions, format, or size, and left `image-text` named only in the `Commands:` reference line. That inverted the block's own design intent, recorded in its docblock: the failure shapes are what an agent matches against at the moment it decides to read, and the reference list is what it consults afterwards. Reading the text in a screenshot, a diagram, or a scan is the single most common reason to open an image at all, so the one case most likely to fire had no recognizable shape to fire on. Found by reading the rendered gate rather than by a failing test -- the existing assertions check that named rows are present, so nothing in the suite could have reported a row that was never written. See [src/bridges/guidance_block.ts](src/bridges/guidance_block.ts), [.github/copilot-instructions.md](.github/copilot-instructions.md).
- **A `symbol` miss on a name that really is a nested JSON/YAML key now names the exact dot-path instead of answering with a confident negative.** JSON and YAML files are indexed only at depth 1 -- top-level keys become `property` symbols, nested ones deliberately do not, or every manifest would flood bare-name lookups with thousands of `name`/`version`/`type` rows and duplicate `json-query`. Nothing in the miss message said so, so `symbol better-sqlite3` answered `No matches for 'better-sqlite3'` followed by `Did you mean: sql` -- a wrong answer wearing a near-miss suggestion that points away from the real one. One probe was enough to produce a correct-from-evidence, wrong-in-fact conclusion that JSON files have no token-goat path at all. The miss now resolves the name against the project's already-indexed JSON/YAML files and, only when it genuinely exists as a key at depth 2 or deeper, appends the file, the dot-path, and the `json-query`/`yaml-query` command that reads it, copy-pasteable. When the name is not found that way it prints nothing: a generic "JSON keys aren't symbols" line would fire on nearly every miss in nearly every project and bill itself for a saving it never delivered. Appended alongside the `Did you mean` suggestion rather than replacing it, since that is the case most in need of correcting. Cost is bounded by file size (128 KiB, which skips generated lockfiles unread), file count (12) and node count, uses the symbol scan the miss path already performed rather than a second query or a filesystem walk, and swallows parse errors so a malformed manifest cannot turn a clean miss into an error; measured at about +13 ms on a 445 ms `symbol` miss in this repo, paid only on a query that already failed. `--json` output is unchanged. See [src/read_commands.ts](src/read_commands.ts), [tests/guards/structured_data_discoverability.test.ts](tests/guards/structured_data_discoverability.test.ts).
